sections.title: Communication
sections.covers: Closed & open-ended questions · 5 levels of communication · 3 V's · social, personal & intimate space

q.q: A patient arrives in obvious respiratory distress. Which question is the MOST appropriate first question for the RT to ask?
o: "Are you short of breath right now?"
"Tell me about your breathing over the last few weeks."
"You're feeling a little better now that you're here, aren't you?"
"When did this start, how bad is it, and have you used your inhaler?"
q.e: Closed-ended questions get specific information fast, which is what you need with a patient in distress. "You're feeling a little better…, aren't you?" is a leading question, and asking several things at once is a compound question — avoid both.

q.q: Which statement BEST describes open-ended questions?
o: They let the patient tell their story and give broader information
They produce a yes/no answer or a single specific piece of data
They give limited insight but deliver specific information quickly
They nudge the patient toward the answer the RT is hoping for
q.e: Open-ended questions give broader information and often uncover things you would not have thought to ask. Yes/no answers and fast specific data describe closed-ended questions; nudging toward an answer describes a leading question.

q.q: "You're feeling better after that treatment, aren't you?" is an example of which type of question?
q.e: A leading question nudges the patient toward the answer you want and produces false or slanted information. Avoid it.

q.q: Asking "Do you have a cough, fever, and chest pain?" is a poor technique because:
o: It is compound — one "yes" can't be tied to any item
It is open-ended, so the answer takes too long to get
It is leading — it suggests the answer the RT wants
It is cliché conversation that yields no useful data
q.e: Compound questions ask several things at once, so the answer cannot be tied to any one item.

q.q: Which interview sequence reflects the strategy taught in the communication lecture?
o: Start broad with an open-ended question, then narrow down with closed-ended questions
Start with closed-ended questions, then finish with one open-ended question
Use only closed-ended questions to save time
Use only open-ended questions to build rapport
q.e: Start broad, then narrow: "Tell me about your cough" → "When did it start?" → "Is it productive?" → "What color is the sputum?" Summary sequence: Open-ended → Closed-ended → Clarify → Silence/Facilitation → Summarize/Confirm.

q.q: A patient says, "How are you today?" and the RT replies, "Fine." This exchange is which level of communication?
q.e: Level 5 is the most superficial: basic social interaction with little meaningful information. It is still useful, because it is often how rapport begins.

q.q: A patient tells you, "I'm scared I'll end up on the ventilator again." Which level of communication is this?
q.e: Level 2 is when the patient trusts you enough to say how they actually feel.

q.q: "I don't think these treatments are helping" represents which level of communication?
q.e: Level 3 is the patient sharing what they think or believe. Explore it rather than correct it.

q.q: "I've been coughing for three days and I'm on 2 liters at home" is which level of communication?
q.e: Level 4 is exchanging objective information. Most routine healthcare communication happens here.

q.q: Which levels of communication are the therapeutic "sweet spot" the RT should aim to reach with a patient?
q.e: The RT must move beyond superficial Levels 4–5 and build enough trust to reach meaningful therapeutic communication, usually Levels 2–3.

q.q: A patient shares a deep fear with the RT (Level 2). What is the appropriate RT response?
o: Respond therapeutically without sharing the RT's own fears
Share a personal fear of equal depth to build trust with the patient
Redirect the patient back to Level 4 facts to keep things professional
Move the conversation up to Level 1 peak communication
q.e: The patient may communicate at Level 2, but the RT does not reciprocate at Level 2. Patient self-disclosure gets a therapeutic response. Level 1 is reserved for close personal relationships, not the RT–patient relationship.

q.q: Which chain summarizes the goal of therapeutic communication?
q.e: The overall goal is relationships built on honesty, trust and respect; the chain to remember is Rapport → Trust → Cooperation.

q.q: According to the 3 V's of communication, what percentage of a message is conveyed by the VISUAL component?
q.e: Verbal 7% (words), Vocal 38% (tone, volume, pitch, rate), Visual 55% (facial expression, gestures, posture, body language).

q.q: Tone, volume, pitch and rate of speech belong to which of the 3 V's, and what percentage is it?
q.e: Vocal = 38%. Verbal (the words themselves) = 7%. Visual (body language) = 55%.

q.q: According to the 3 V's model, how much of communication is nonverbal?
q.e: Vocal 38% + Visual 55% = 93% nonverbal. Only the words (7%) are verbal.

q.q: An RT tells an anxious patient "Take your time, I'm here with you" while checking a watch and standing by the door. What is the problem?
o: The verbal message is not congruent with the vocal and visual messages
The RT used a closed-ended question
The RT entered the patient's intimate space without permission
q.e: When verbal and nonverbal messages conflict, people rely on the vocal and visual cues. Verbal + Vocal + Visual must be congruent.

q.q: The 7 / 38 / 55 percentages come from Mehrabian's research. What is the caveat the instructor stresses?
o: They apply to feelings and attitudes when verbal and nonverbal signals conflict
They apply to all spoken communication, including ventilator orders
They were measured only in critically ill ICU patients
They apply only to written communication in the chart
q.e: Mehrabian himself said the formula does not apply to communication generally. Memorize 7/38/55 for the exam, but know it is an overgeneralization.

q.q: What is the distance of INTIMATE space?
q.e: Intimate space is 1"–18" (0–1.5 ft), normally reserved for very close relationships. The deck lists it both ways — they are the same distance.

q.q: What distance is PERSONAL space, used for one-on-one patient interviews and patient education?
q.e: Personal space = 1.5–4 ft, the comfortable distance for one-on-one conversation, interviews and education.

q.q: What distance is SOCIAL space?
q.e: Social space = 4–12 ft: groups, coworkers, meetings and less personal conversations. Public space is 12–25 ft.

q.q: An RT is about to auscultate breath sounds. What is the MOST appropriate action before entering the patient's intimate space?
o: Explain what you are going to do and ask permission
Enter quickly so the patient has less time to become anxious
Stay in social space and ask the patient to describe their breath sounds
Ask a family member for consent
q.e: RTs enter intimate space constantly (suctioning, auscultation, BiPAP masks, ABGs). The communication skill is what you do before you enter: explain and ask permission.

q.q: Proxemics is BEST defined as:
o: The use and interpretation of space and its effect on communication
The study of facial expressions, gestures and body posture
The tone, pitch, volume and rate of the speaking voice
The documentation of patient communication in the record
q.e: Proxemics is the use and interpretation of space. The zones are conceptual, not rigid, and vary with culture, relationship, situation and patient condition.

sections.title: Burn and Inhalation Injury
sections.covers: Burns (BSA / Rule of Nines) · degrees of burns · static and dynamic lung compliance ranges

q.q: Using the Rule of Nines, what %TBSA is assigned to the head and neck of an adult?
q.e: Head & neck = 9%. Each arm 9%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18%, each leg 18%, perineum 1% — total 100%.

q.q: Using the Rule of Nines, what %TBSA is ONE entire leg in an adult?
q.e: Each leg = 18% (Hess splits it as thigh 9% + leg-and-foot 9%).

q.q: An adult has burns to the entire anterior trunk and the entire right arm. What is the %TBSA burned?
q.e: Anterior trunk 18% + right arm 9% = 27% TBSA (the deck's own worked example).

q.q: An adult has burns to both entire arms and the entire posterior trunk. Estimate the %TBSA.
Which region is assigned 1% in the Rule of Nines?
q.e: The perineum (genitals) is the 1% that brings the multiples of 9 to 100%.

q.q: A burn greater than what %TBSA is defined as a major burn?
q.e: A major burn is defined as >20% TBSA.

q.q: What is the single most important reason to estimate %TBSA accurately?
o: It determines the ventilator mode to use
It determines the degree of the burn
It determines whether an ABG is needed
q.e: %TBSA plus patient weight determines initial fluid resuscitation. The deck's example rate is 4 mL/kg/%TBSA for adults, with half given in the first 8 hours post-burn.

q.q: Using the deck's resuscitation rate of 4 mL/kg/%TBSA, how much of the 24-hour volume is given in the first 8 hours post-burn?
q.e: Half of the calculated volume is given in the first 8 hours post-burn.

q.q: A 70-kg adult has 30% TBSA burns. Using 4 mL/kg/%TBSA, what is the total calculated resuscitation volume, and how much is given in the first 8 hours?
o: 8,400 mL total; 4,200 mL in the first 8 hours
2,100 mL total; 1,050 mL in the first 8 hours
8,400 mL total; 2,800 mL in the first 8 hours
4,200 mL total; 2,100 mL in the first 8 hours
q.e: 4 × 70 × 30 = 8,400 mL. Half (4,200 mL) in the first 8 hours.

q.q: For estimating small or scattered burns, the patient's palm (including fingers) is approximately what %TBSA?
q.e: Palm ≈ 1% TBSA. The deck says palm including fingers; Hess says palmar surface without fingers. Answer the deck's version on a 202 exam.

q.q: Why is the Rule of Nines NOT used for a small child?
o: A child's head is proportionally larger and legs smaller, so an age-adjusted chart is used
Children rarely get full-thickness burns, so depth matters more than extent
The Rule of Nines overestimates fluid needs, so children get half the calculated volume
Children's burns are always estimated with the palm method instead of a chart
q.e: The Rule of Nines is an adult estimate. The Lund-Browder chart is age-specific; Hess calls it the preferred method.

q.q: Which burn-extent method does Hess call "the preferred method"?
q.e: Hess: the Lund-Browder chart is the preferred method because it is age-specific. The Rule of Nines is "a rough method of estimation."

q.q: A burn that involves only the epidermis and is red, dry, painful, without blisters (like a sunburn) is:
q.e: First degree = epidermis only; red, dry, painful, no blisters; heals in about 7 days.

q.q: A hot-water scald with blisters that is VERY painful and involves the epidermis plus superficial dermis is:
q.e: Superficial partial-thickness: epidermis + superficial dermis, blisters, very painful, heals in 10–21 days with no scar.

q.q: A burn that is charred, pale and leathery, involves the entire epidermis and dermis, and has little or no pain is:
q.e: Full-thickness burns destroy the sensory nerve endings, so there is little or no pain. They need skin grafts.

q.q: Why can a 2nd-degree burn be MORE painful than a 3rd-degree burn?
o: Partial-thickness burns leave nerve endings intact
2nd-degree burns always cover more of the body
3rd-degree burns are given more pain medication
2nd-degree burns extend down into the muscle
q.e: In a full-thickness burn the sensory nerve endings are destroyed; in a partial-thickness burn they are intact. (The partial-thickness skin around a full-thickness burn still hurts.)

q.q: A burn that extends beyond the skin into fat, muscle, tendon or bone is:
q.e: Fourth degree extends into deep structures; months of healing, severe scarring, multiple grafts.

q.q: Which burn depth requires skin grafts?
q.e: The concept to remember: superficial heals fast, deeper heals slowly with scarring, full-thickness needs surgery (grafts).

q.q: Which burn zone is salvageable and is what good fluid resuscitation protects?
q.e: Coagulation (center) = dead; stasis (middle) = maybe, decreased perfusion, salvageable; hyperemia (outer) = recovers spontaneously.

q.q: Per the burn deck's pulmonary mechanics slide, normal STATIC compliance is:
q.e: Deck: static compliance 70–100 mL/cm H₂O; lung compliance ("how easily the lungs expand") 50–100 mL/cm H₂O.

q.q: Per the burn deck, normal lung compliance ("how easily the lungs expand") is:
q.e: Deck: lung compliance 50–100 mL/cm H₂O. This matches Hess's "acceptable CRS" for ventilated patients (50–100).

q.q: Which formula calculates STATIC compliance?
q.e: Cstatic = VT ÷ (Pplat − PEEP). Cdynamic = VT ÷ (PIP − PEEP).

q.q: Which formula calculates DYNAMIC compliance?
q.e: Cdyn uses peak pressure, so it includes airway resistance; Cstat uses plateau pressure.

q.q: A ventilated patient has VT 500 mL, Pplat 30 cm H₂O and PEEP 5 cm H₂O. What is the static compliance?
q.e: 500 ÷ (30 − 5) = 500 ÷ 25 = 20 mL/cm H₂O — well below normal.

q.q: A ventilated patient has VT 450 mL, PIP 35 cm H₂O, Pplat 25 cm H₂O, PEEP 10 cm H₂O. What is the dynamic compliance?
q.e: Cdyn = 450 ÷ (35 − 10) = 18 mL/cm H₂O. (Static would be 450 ÷ 15 = 30.)

q.q: What is the published normal range for DYNAMIC compliance?
o: None is published — it is a comparative value always lower than static
70–100 mL/cm H₂O, the same as static compliance
50–100 mL/cm H₂O, the deck's lung compliance range
30–40 mL/cm H₂O, because resistance lowers it
q.e: No source gives a dynamic compliance range. Cdyn bundles compliance with resistance and moves with flow, tube size and secretions. If a question asks for a normal compliance range, it wants the static one.

q.q: How does inhalation injury or a major burn affect lung compliance?
o: Decreases it — permeability rises and pulmonary edema develops
Increases it — the lungs become hyperinflated from air trapping
No effect — compliance changes only with a chest wall burn
Increases it — surfactant production rises after the injury
q.e: Inflammation → ↑ permeability → pulmonary edema → ↓ compliance and impaired oxygenation (ARDS-like).

q.q: A patient with a circumferential chest burn has rising ventilator pressures and poor chest expansion. What procedure may be needed?
q.e: Rigid eschar plus edema mechanically restricts chest expansion (↓ compliance). Escharotomy lets the thorax expand.

q.q: For a burn patient with falling compliance, which ventilator strategy protects against VILI?
o: VT ≈ 6 mL/kg PBW with plateau pressure ≤ 30 cm H₂O
VT 10–12 mL/kg PBW with plateau pressure ≤ 40 cm H₂O
VT 6 mL/kg actual body weight with no plateau limit
Zero PEEP to lower mean airway pressure
q.e: Low VT ≈ 6 mL/kg PBW, Pplat ≤ 30 cm H₂O, and appropriate PEEP.

sections.title: ECMO
sections.covers: Access points · VV vs VA · inclusion criteria · tracking and guidelines

q.q: What is the key difference between VV ECMO and VA ECMO?
o: VV = respiratory failure; VA = cardiac and cardiopulmonary failure
VV = cardiac failure; VA = respiratory failure only
VV = CO₂ removal only; VA = oxygenation only
VV = neonates only; VA = adults only
q.e: Hess: "VV ECMO provides support for respiratory failure. VA ECMO provides support for cardiac and cardiopulmonary failure." Where the blood is returned is the whole difference.

q.q: A patient with severe ARDS also has cardiogenic shock with poor cardiac output. Which ECMO configuration is indicated?
o: VV ECMO with a dual-lumen catheter
q.e: VV "requires an adequate cardiac function." If the heart cannot do its job, VV is not an option — VA provides oxygenation, CO₂ removal AND perfusion.

q.q: Which ECMO configuration REQUIRES adequate cardiac function?
q.e: VV supports only gas exchange; the patient's own heart must pump the oxygenated blood. VA also provides perfusion.

q.q: Why is VV ECMO preferred over VA for adult respiratory failure?
o: Simplicity and a more favorable safety profile
It achieves higher PaO₂ in the upper body
q.e: Hess: VV is preferred "both for simplicity and for its more favourable safety profile." VA is a salvage technique in adult respiratory failure.

q.q: Which risk is specifically associated with VA ECMO rather than VV?
o: Coronary, brain and upper-body ischemia, and more strokes
Recirculation of oxygenated blood back into the circuit
Bleeding at the cannulation site from anticoagulation
Hemolysis from high pump flow through the oxygenator
q.e: Hess lists coronary, brain and upper-body ischemia, increased stroke risk and more vascular complications for VA. Oxygenated blood returned to the femoral artery flows against the heart's own output.

q.q: On ECMO, which setting is the primary control for CO₂ removal?
q.e: CO₂ clearance depends on the diffusion gradient into the sweep gas. Sweep gas is the knob for CO₂; blood flow is the knob for oxygenation.

q.q: On ECMO, which setting is the primary control for oxygenation?
q.e: Blood flow through the oxygenator controls oxygenation; sweep gas controls CO₂.

q.q: In dual-site VV ECMO, where are the cannulas typically placed?
o: Femoral vein drainage; return to the right IJ or other femoral vein
Femoral vein drainage; return to the femoral artery
Right atrial drainage; return to the ascending aorta
Subclavian artery drainage; return to the femoral vein
q.e: VV dual-site: drainage cannula in a femoral vein, return in the right IJ or the contralateral femoral vein. Femoral vein → femoral artery is VA.

q.q: Where is a single-site dual-lumen VV ECMO catheter usually placed?
q.e: Usually the right IJ (it can also go in the left subclavian vein). It drains from the SVC and IVC and returns to the right atrium.

q.q: What is an advantage of single-site (dual-lumen) VV cannulation?
o: Less vessel trauma and infection, and more wakefulness and mobility
Higher blood flows than dual-site cannulation can reach
Cardiac support in addition to gas exchange
Placement without fluoroscopy or echo guidance
q.e: Single-site reduces vessel trauma and infection risk and makes awake, mobile ECMO possible. It cannot reach the higher flows of dual-site, and it should be placed under fluoroscopy or TEE.

q.q: What is the typical peripheral cannulation for VA ECMO?
o: Venous drainage from the femoral vein; return to the femoral artery
Drainage from the femoral vein; return to the right IJ vein
Dual-lumen catheter in the right IJ
Drainage from the radial artery; return to the femoral vein
q.e: VA: femoral vein drainage, femoral artery return. Open-chest cannulation is also used.

q.q: On VV ECMO, the blood in the venous drainage tubing turns bright red and the SpO₂ falls. What is the most likely problem?
q.e: Recirculation = oxygenated blood going back into the circuit instead of to the patient. Signs: drainage blood brighter red, rising SvO₂; significant when SpO₂ drops.

q.q: What is the correct response to significant recirculation on VV ECMO?
o: Decrease ECMO flow and confirm cannula position
Increase ECMO flow to push more blood to the patient
Increase sweep gas to clear the extra CO₂
Convert immediately to VA ECMO for cardiac support
q.e: Causes include improper cannula position, hypovolemia, excess flows or decreased cardiac output. Fix: decrease flow and confirm cannula position.

q.q: ECMO should be reserved for which patients?
o: Patients with a reversible process, or as a bridge to lung transplant
Any patient whose P/F ratio stays below 300 on the ventilator
Patients with multiorgan failure who have exhausted other options
Any patient who has failed a trial of noninvasive ventilation
q.e: The gate: a reversible process, or a successful bridge to transplant in end-stage lung disease.

q.q: What is the MOST common indication for VV ECMO?
q.e: Severe ARDS is the most common VV indication. Others: status asthmaticus, PE, airway compression, air-leak syndromes, PPHN, congenital airway anomalies.

q.q: Which formula is the Oxygenation Index used to consider ECMO?
q.e: OI = (mean airway pressure × FiO₂ × 100) ÷ PaO₂. A higher OI means worse oxygenation.

q.q: A neonate has P̄aw 20 cm H₂O, FiO₂ 1.0 and PaO₂ 50 mm Hg. What is the Oxygenation Index, and does it fall in ELSO's initiation range?
q.e: OI = (20 × 1.0 × 100) ÷ 50 = 40. ELSO recommends initiation in neonates at OI 20–40; OI ≥ 33 is where lung-injury risk outweighs ECMO risk.

q.q: At what Oxygenation Index did one study find that the risk of lung injury outweighs the risk of ECMO?
q.e: OI ≥ 33. ELSO's neonatal initiation range is OI 20–40.

q.q: What does the Murray Lung Injury Score consider?
o: PaO₂/FiO₂, chest x-ray infiltrates, lung compliance and PEEP
Heart rate, blood pressure, urine output and GCS
pH, PaCO₂, HCO₃⁻ and base excess
q.e: Murray LIS uses P/F, infiltrate severity, compliance and PEEP; scored 0–4, with 4 the most severe ARDS. CESAR enrolled LIS > 3.

q.q: ELSO guidelines recommend initiating ECMO once predicted mortality reaches:
q.e: ELSO: 50–80%. Hess calls this "arbitrary" and warns that patients in that band often have multisystem organ failure and may be LESS likely to benefit.

q.q: What is ELSO?
o: The Extracorporeal Life Support Organization, which tracks ECMO outcomes
The ECMO Lung Severity Outcome score used to decide on initiation
The European Lung Support Outcomes trial that proved ECMO's benefit
The Extracorporeal Lung Support Oxygenator used in most circuits
q.e: ELSO tracks ECMO volume and outcomes. Adult cases now exceed neonatal cases for the first time since the 1970s.

q.q: What is the cumulative survival for all respiratory ECMO patients in the ELSO registry?
q.e: 61%, decreasing with age. Near-fatal asthma on ECMO survives at 84% (younger, single-organ, reversible).

q.q: What is the MOST common complication of ECMO?
q.e: "Bleeding is the most common complication related to ECMO," usually at the cannulation or surgical site. Transfusion threshold Hb 7–8 g/dL.

q.q: Which group of ECMO patients has particularly good outcomes (about 84% survival)?
q.e: Asthma patients tend to be younger, with single-organ dysfunction and a readily reversible cause. Repeat ECMO courses have poor outcomes.

q.q: Which conditions does the 202 deck ADD (with an asterisk) to Hess's ECMO indication list?
q.e: The deck reproduces Hess's list and marks smoke inhalation and severe pneumonia with an asterisk. An asterisk on the instructor's slide outweighs an omission in the book.

q.q: What is the median duration of ECMO support for ARDS?
q.e: Median 9–15 days in ARDS; asthma recovers much faster.

sections.title: Pulmonary Rehabilitation
sections.covers: Adequate arterial oxygenation limits · training intensity · frequency of training and reassessment · 6MWT · breathing patterns

q.q: During exercise, what is the minimum adequate arterial oxygenation (the "floor") used in O₂ titration?
q.e: The decision point is SpO₂ 88% / PaO₂ 55 torr.

q.q: During an O₂ titration with exercise, the patient's SpO₂ falls to 86% at peak activity. What should the RT do?
o: Increase O₂ by 1 L/min until SpO₂ is ≥ 88%
Stop the titration and end the test
q.e: If SpO₂ drops ≥ 2% or falls below 88%, increase O₂ by 1 L/min until SpO₂ ≥ 88%. The resulting flow is what the physician prescribes for activity.

q.q: At what saturation should the O₂ titration with exercise be STOPPED entirely?
q.e: Stop the titration if SaO₂ drops below 85%. Don't start the test if resting SpO₂ is below 85% on room air.

q.q: A patient's resting SpO₂ on room air is 83%. What should the RT do about the planned O₂ titration exercise test?
o: Start the test on room air
Start the test and stop at SpO₂ 80%
q.e: Do not start the test if resting SpO₂ is less than 85% on room air.

q.q: During O₂ titration, what target SpO₂ does the AARC recommend for an extra margin of safety?
q.e: AARC recommends a titration target of 93% for extra safety margin.

q.q: Which piece of equipment is NOT recommended for O₂ titration with exercise?
q.e: O₂ needs must be established while the patient carries the portable system they actually use. A treadmill, step test or 6MWT can be used.

q.q: What is the target heart rate range for pulmonary rehab training?
q.e: Target HR = 60–75% of predicted HRmax (220 − age) for optimal cardiovascular benefit.

q.q: What is the training target heart rate for a 70-year-old pulmonary rehab patient?
What is the training target heart rate for a 60-year-old pulmonary rehab patient?
One MET is equal to:
q.e: 1 MET = 3.5 mL O₂ consumption per kg per minute, roughly resting O₂ consumption.

q.q: Exercise capacity is considered REDUCED if the patient cannot reach:
q.e: Reduced exercise capacity: unable to reach ≥ 5 METs, or VO₂max < 15 mL/kg/min.

q.q: The Modified Borg Scale rates dyspnea or exertion on what scale?
q.e: Modified Borg: 0 (nothing at all) to 10 (maximal), always tied to a predefined level of activity.

q.q: On the Modified Borg Scale, a rating of 3 for shortness of breath means:
q.e: 2 = slight, 3 = moderate, 4 = somewhat severe, 5 = severe, 10 = maximal.

q.q: During a rehab exercise session, which finding requires the RT to STOP the exercise?
o: Heart rate at 65% of predicted maximum
q.e: Stop for angina, muscle cramps, severe fatigue, excessive dyspnea, or other signs of distress.

q.q: When the 6MWT is used to assess a treatment, what improvement in distance indicates the treatment was effective?
q.e: Expect at least a 10–20% improvement in 6MWD to call a treatment effective.

q.q: The 6MWT or exercise-capacity evaluation is used for all of the following rehab purposes EXCEPT:
q.e: The four uses: screen, establish baseline, monitor progress, measure improvement. The 6MWT does not measure O₂ uptake.

q.q: In Heuer's sample COPD action plan, how often should the patient walk?
q.e: Walk around the block (about 1/3 mile), 4× per week, with follow-up at the next office visit in 3 months.

q.q: What is the inspiratory muscle training (IMT) schedule Heuer specifies?
q.e: IMT: 1–2 sessions/day, 30 min total/day, 4–6 days/week; increase intensity 5% of PImax/week; at least 5 weeks for functional improvement.

q.q: What happens to rehab benefits if the patient stops training?
q.e: Patients progressively lose health-related benefit if they stop training — the argument for continuing indefinitely.

q.q: What does the 6-minute walk test measure?
o: The distance walked on a flat surface in 6 minutes
The underlying cause of the patient's dyspnea
The exercise level where blood lactate begins to rise
q.e: The outcome is the 6-minute walk distance (6MWD). It does not measure O₂ uptake or identify the cause of dyspnea — use a cardiopulmonary exercise test for that.

q.q: How long must the 6MWT walking course be, per ATS standards?
q.e: 30 m, with a marked start and turnaround and distance marked in 3-meter increments.

q.q: Which is an ABSOLUTE contraindication to a 6MWT?
o: MI or unstable angina in the previous month
q.e: Absolute: MI or unstable angina in the month before. Relative: resting HR > 120, systolic BP > 180, diastolic BP > 100.

q.q: A patient's resting heart rate is 124 beats/min before a scheduled 6MWT. This is:
o: An indication to walk with the patient
q.e: Resting HR > 120 is a relative contraindication (as are systolic > 180 and diastolic > 100).

q.q: How long should the patient rest before starting a 6MWT?
q.e: Patient sits at rest for at least 10 minutes while vital signs are gathered. Avoid vigorous exercise for 2 hours before testing.

q.q: During a 6MWT, what is the correct role of the RT?
o: Stay at the start line, tally laps, and encourage at the end of each minute
Walk beside the patient to keep a steady, safe pace throughout
Encourage the patient continuously in whatever words motivate them
Stop the patient at 5 minutes to recheck vitals, then finish the walk
q.e: Encouragement is standardized: at the end of each minute, stating the remaining time. Walking alongside would pace the patient and invalidate the result.

q.q: A patient on home O₂ is scheduled for a 6MWT. How should oxygen be handled?
o: Use the prescribed flow on the patient's usual portable system
Remove the oxygen so the true room-air distance is measured
Switch to 100% O₂ by nonrebreather for safety
Double the prescribed flow to prevent desaturation
q.e: Patients on O₂ use their prescribed flow and the same portable system they normally use.

q.q: Which finding requires the RT to STOP a 6MWT immediately?
o: Diaphoresis with a pale, ashen appearance
q.e: Stop for chest pain, severe dyspnea, leg cramps, staggering, diaphoresis, or pale/ashen appearance.

q.q: A 6MWD below what distance screens as abnormal functional capacity?
q.e: < 500–600 m screens abnormal; the patient should undergo further pulmonary and cardiac testing.

q.q: In a patient with pulmonary arterial hypertension, a 6MWD below what distance is associated with higher mortality?
q.e: < 330 m in PAH is the mortality threshold — the one hard mortality number Heuer gives for the 6MWT.

q.q: Which emergency equipment must be immediately available during a 6MWT?
o: Oxygen, an AED and a telephone
q.e: Oxygen, an AED and a telephone must be immediately accessible.

q.q: Pursed-lip breathing is BEST described as:
o: An expiratory technique that creates back-pressure to keep airways open
An inspiratory technique that strengthens the diaphragm against a load
An accessory-muscle breathing pattern that rehab tries to undo
A breathing pattern that deliberately lowers the PaCO₂
q.e: Pursed-lip breathing prolongs exhalation (aim for expiratory time 2–3× inspiration), prevents airway collapse, slows the rate, and may reduce dyspnea — especially in COPD.

q.q: When teaching pursed-lip breathing, the patient should aim for an expiratory time that is:
o: At least 2–3 times longer than inspiration
At least 5 times longer than inspiration
q.e: Expiratory time at least 2 to 3 times longer than inspiration.

q.q: Diaphragmatic breathing is BEST described as:
o: An inspiratory exercise that raises VT, lowers rate, and reduces accessory muscle use
An expiratory technique that creates back-pressure to prevent airway collapse
An upper-chest pattern driven by the scalenes and sternocleidomastoids
A technique that swallows air into the lungs using the throat muscles
q.e: Diaphragmatic breathing promotes diaphragm excursion, increases VT, decreases rate, and reduces accessory muscle use. Patient in semi-Fowler's; inhale slowly through the nose and push out against the RT's hand.

q.q: Which breathing technique must be taught BEFORE starting inspiratory muscle training?
q.e: Diaphragmatic breathing must be taught before IMT.

q.q: Thoracic (upper-chest) breathing uses which muscles?
o: Sternocleidomastoid, scalenes, upper trapezius, pectoralis major
Diaphragm with the external intercostals only
Internal intercostals and the abdominal muscles
Glossopharyngeal muscles of the throat and tongue
q.e: Thoracic breathing is driven by the accessory muscles. It is the abnormal, high-work pattern rehab tries to undo, not a technique.

q.q: Increased thoracic (accessory muscle) breathing at rest is typically seen in:
o: Emphysema and any increased work of breathing
Normal quiet breathing in a healthy adult
Metabolic alkalosis with a normal PaCO₂
q.e: Seen in emphysema, any increased WOB, and impaired diaphragm function (spinal cord injury, neuromuscular disease).

q.q: Hyperventilation is defined as:
o: Ventilation in excess of metabolic need, so PaCO₂ falls below 35 torr
Ventilation below metabolic need, so PaCO₂ rises above 45 torr
Deep breathing with a normal PaCO₂
q.e: Hyper- and hypoventilation are acid-base states defined by PaCO₂, not by how fast the patient looks like they are breathing. Normal PaCO₂ = 35–45 torr.

q.q: A patient doing incentive spirometry too quickly reports lightheadedness and tingling fingers. What is happening, and what should the RT do?
o: Hyperventilation — coach slower breathing with pauses
Hypoxemia — stop therapy and call a rapid response
q.e: Too-fast IS or IPPB causes hyperventilation: ↓ PaCO₂ → respiratory alkalosis, with dizziness and paresthesia. Coach slower breathing (fewer than 8–10/min) with pauses.

q.q: What acid-base disturbance does hyperventilation cause?
q.e: ↓ PaCO₂ → ↑ pH → respiratory alkalosis.

q.q: What acid-base disturbance does hypoventilation cause?
o: Respiratory acidosis with a lower PaO₂
Respiratory alkalosis with a higher PaO₂
q.e: ↑ PaCO₂ → ↓ pH (respiratory acidosis), and because CO₂ displaces O₂ in the alveolus, PaO₂ falls too.

q.q: A COPD patient on high-flow O₂ becomes drowsy and the PaCO₂ rises. What O₂ approach does Heuer recommend?
o: Target PaO₂ 55–60 torr with a 28% air-entrainment device
Switch to a nonrebreather to correct the hypoxemia fully
Remove all oxygen until the PaCO₂ normalizes
Start CPAP alone to correct the hypoventilation
q.e: This is O₂-induced hypoventilation. Target PaO₂ 55–60 torr with a 28% air-entrainment device. CPAP alone does not overcome hypoventilation — bilevel support is needed.

q.q: In a traumatic brain injury patient, how does hypercapnia affect ICP?
o: Decreases ICP by lowering blood pressure
q.e: Hypercapnia → cerebral vasodilation → ↑ ICP. Hypocapnia → vasoconstriction → ↓ ICP, but with ischemia risk, so routine hyperventilation is not recommended.

sections.title: Renal Failure — Neuro & A&P
sections.covers: Acetylcholine · causes of increased and decreased ICP · CNS, PNS, ANS and neurotransmitters · neurons · medulla oblongata · spinal cord

q.q: Acetylcholine is the primary neurotransmitter of which division of the autonomic nervous system?
o: Neither — it is only a CNS transmitter
q.e: Ach is the parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) neurotransmitter. The two PNS neurotransmitters are acetylcholine and norepinephrine.

q.q: What enzyme inactivates acetylcholine?
q.e: Ach is inactivated by cholinesterase. Norepinephrine is terminated by reuptake, COMT and MAO.

q.q: Acetylcholine acts on which two receptor families?
q.e: Cholinergic receptors are muscarinic (M1–M5) and nicotinic. Alpha, beta and dopaminergic receptors are adrenergic (sympathetic).

q.q: Which muscarinic receptor subtype is found on airway smooth muscle?
q.e: M3 = airway smooth muscle (and blood vessels); M2 = heart; M1 on parasympathetic ganglia.

q.q: Stimulation of muscarinic receptors by acetylcholine in the lungs causes:
q.e: Parasympathetic/Ach effects: ↓ HR, bronchoconstriction, ↑ secretions, miosis, ↑ GI motility.

q.q: At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine binds which receptor type to cause skeletal muscle contraction?
q.e: At the NMJ, Ach binds nicotinic end-plate receptors → depolarization → contraction. This is the somatic (voluntary) system, not autonomic.

q.q: Methacholine, used in the bronchoprovocation test, is classified as a:
q.e: Methacholine mimics Ach (direct-acting cholinergic) and causes bronchoconstriction — the basis of the methacholine challenge.

q.q: Neostigmine works by:
o: Inhibiting cholinesterase so more acetylcholine accumulates
Blocking muscarinic receptors so acetylcholine cannot bind
Binding the Ach receptor directly the way methacholine does
Stimulating beta-2 receptors to relax airway smooth muscle
q.e: Neostigmine is an indirect-acting cholinergic. It treats myasthenia gravis and reverses nondepolarizing paralytics.

q.q: Atropine is BEST described as:
o: An anticholinergic that blocks muscarinic receptors
A cholinesterase inhibitor that raises acetylcholine
A sympathomimetic that stimulates beta receptors
q.e: Atropine is a competitive antagonist → bronchodilation, drying of secretions, treats bradycardia and organophosphate poisoning.

q.q: Succinylcholine differs from vecuronium because succinylcholine:
o: It binds and activates the receptor, giving short-acting paralysis
It blocks the receptor without activating it, giving long paralysis
It acts only on muscarinic receptors in the airway smooth muscle
It works in the CNS and has no effect at the neuromuscular junction
q.e: Depolarizing (succinylcholine): binds AND activates → end plate becomes refractory → short-acting, used for intubation. Nondepolarizing (vecuronium, cisatracurium): block the receptor → prolonged paralysis.

q.q: In myasthenia gravis, what blocks acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction?
q.e: MG = anti-AchR antibodies → fatigability. (Demyelination is Guillain-Barré.)

q.q: A myasthenia gravis patient worsens after Tensilon, with diaphoresis, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm and miosis. What is this and what treats it?
q.e: Improves with Tensilon = myasthenic crisis. Worsens = cholinergic crisis (too much Ach); atropine is the treatment.

q.q: What is the normal ICP in a supine healthy adult?
q.e: Normal ICP 10–15 mm Hg. > 20 for more than 5–10 min is abnormally high; > 25 prolonged is critical.

q.q: An ICP above what value for more than 5–10 minutes is considered abnormally high?
q.e: > 20 mm Hg for more than 5–10 min is abnormal/unsafe. TBI goal: ICP < 20 mm Hg.

q.q: How is cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) calculated, and what is the TBI goal?
o: CPP = MAP − ICP; goal ≥ 60 mm Hg
CPP = ICP − MAP; goal ≥ 20 mm Hg
CPP = MAP + ICP; goal ≥ 90 mm Hg
CPP = SBP − ICP; goal ≥ 100 mm Hg
q.e: CPP = MAP − ICP. TBI goals: ICP < 20, CPP ≥ 60, MAP > 75 mm Hg.

q.q: A TBI patient has MAP 80 mm Hg and ICP 25 mm Hg. What is the CPP, and is it acceptable?
o: 55 mm Hg — below the goal of ≥ 60
q.e: CPP = 80 − 25 = 55 mm Hg, below the ≥ 60 goal. The ICP (25) is also above the < 20 goal.

q.q: Which of the following DECREASES ICP?
o: Elevating the head of the bed 30–40°
q.e: Head elevation, decreased CSF volume, hyperventilation/hypocapnia, mannitol, ventricular drainage and sedation lower ICP.

q.q: Which of the following INCREASES ICP?
q.e: CO₂ causes cerebral vasodilation → ↑ ICP. Hypoxia, high PEEP, hemorrhage, edema, tumor, hydrocephalus and restricted venous outflow also raise ICP.

q.q: Why does Heuer say to AVOID routine prophylactic hyperventilation in TBI?
o: Hypocapnia constricts cerebral vessels and can cause ischemia
Hypocapnia dilates cerebral vessels and raises ICP further
Hyperventilation causes a dangerous respiratory acidosis
Hyperventilation increases cerebral blood flow too much
q.e: Hyperventilation lowers ICP but risks cerebral ischemia. Use it only before suctioning, in confirmed herniation, or as salvage therapy.

q.q: Which RT procedure is MOST likely to raise ICP in a head-injured patient?
o: Elevating the head of bed to 30°
Keeping the neck in neutral alignment
q.e: Suctioning/coughing, intubation, Trendelenburg, neck flexion/hyperextension, asynchrony, high PEEP and recruitment maneuvers raise ICP.

q.q: Which drug is the osmotic diuretic used to reduce increased ICP?
q.e: Mannitol is "a brain drug, not a lung drug." It pulls water osmotically; caution — it can transiently worsen pulmonary edema and CHF.

q.q: The central nervous system (CNS) consists of:
o: All nerves outside the brain and spinal cord
q.e: CNS = brain + spinal cord ("command center"). PNS = all nerves outside the CNS ("wiring system").

q.q: Neuromuscular blocking agents act on which part of the nervous system?
q.e: NMBAs work on the somatic (voluntary) system at the NMJ. They do not affect the ANS — so they provide no sedation.

q.q: What is the primary neurotransmitter of the sympathetic nervous system?
q.e: Sympathetic = norepinephrine (plus circulating epi/norepi from the adrenal medulla). Parasympathetic = acetylcholine.

q.q: Stimulation of beta-2 receptors in the lungs causes:
q.e: β2 in the lungs → smooth muscle relaxation = bronchodilation. β1 = heart; α1 = vasoconstriction.

q.q: Which receptor is found mainly in the heart and is excitatory?
q.e: β1 excitatory in the heart (↑ HR, force). Note M2 is the parasympathetic heart receptor, which slows it.

q.q: Which set of effects belongs to the SYMPATHETIC (fight-or-flight) system?
o: ↑ HR, bronchodilation, pupil dilation, ↓ GI motility
↓ HR, bronchoconstriction, pupil constriction, ↑ GI motility
q.e: Sympathetic: ↑ HR/BP, bronchodilation, mydriasis, ↓ GI motility, ↑ glucose. The others are parasympathetic.

q.q: The mnemonic SLUD (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation) describes overstimulation of which system?
q.e: SLUD = parasympathetic (cholinergic) overstimulation.

q.q: Parasympathetic nerve fibers originate from which part of the spinal cord?
q.e: Parasympathetic = craniosacral, long preganglionic/short postganglionic. Sympathetic = thoracolumbar, short preganglionic/long postganglionic.

q.q: A drug that is "sympathomimetic" is also called:
q.e: Sympathomimetic = adrenergic; sympatholytic = antiadrenergic. Parasympathomimetic = cholinergic; parasympatholytic = anticholinergic.

q.q: Inhibitory NANC nerves cause bronchodilation using which mediator?
q.e: Inhibitory NANC → bronchodilation via VIP or nitric oxide. Excitatory NANC → bronchoconstriction via substance P.

q.q: What are the three basic parts of a neuron?
q.e: A neuron has a cell body, axons and dendrites.

q.q: Afferent neurons carry signals:
o: From the periphery to the spinal cord (sensory)
From the brain to the effector organ (motor)
q.e: Afferent = Arrives (sensory, periphery → cord). Efferent = Exits (motor, brain/cord → effector).

q.q: The autonomic nervous system is generally considered:
q.e: The ANS is the motor-neuron arm of the PNS and is generally considered efferent.

q.q: Depolarization of a neuron is BEST described as:
o: A shift of the negative internal charge toward positive, so the impulse travels
The return of the cell to its negative resting membrane potential
The release of cholinesterase into the synaptic cleft to end the signal
The blocking of acetylcholine receptors so the muscle cannot contract
q.e: Depolarization = charge moves toward positive, impulse travels. Repolarization = return to negative resting potential.

q.q: In Guillain-Barré syndrome, what is damaged?
o: Myelin sheaths of spinal-root and peripheral nerves
Acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
Respiratory neurons of the medulla oblongata
The phrenic nerve only, sparing all other nerves
q.e: GBS: inflammation destroys myelin → severe weakness and diminished reflexes.

q.q: Which medullary respiratory group is the primary controller of the depth and rate of inspiration?
q.e: The DRG (nucleus tractus solitarius) is the primary controller of the depth and rate of inspiration and sends efferents to the phrenic nerve.

q.q: Where is the pneumotaxic center, and what does it do?
o: Upper pons — the OFF switch for inspiration
Lower pons — the ON switch for inspiration
Medulla — sets the depth of inspiration
Spinal cord — drives the diaphragm directly
q.e: Pneumotaxic = upper pons, controls the stopping point of the inspiratory ramp. Apneustic = lower pons, stimulates inspiration and is normally inhibited by the pneumotaxic center.

q.q: Destruction of the pneumotaxic center produces which breathing pattern?
o: Biot breathing — clusters of breaths with apnea
Cheyne-Stokes — waxing and waning with apnea
q.e: Without the pneumotaxic OFF switch, the apneustic center prevents the inspiratory ramp from shutting off.

q.q: Biot breathing (clusters of rapid breaths with periods of apnea) indicates:
q.e: Biot breathing: medulla damage (stroke, trauma) or brain herniation/↑ ICP. Treat the cause and lower the ICP.

q.q: Waxing and waning tidal volumes with apneic periods (Cheyne-Stokes) point to:
q.e: Cheyne-Stokes = CNS disease or severe CHF; common in TBI.

q.q: A spinal cord injury ABOVE which level typically requires artificial ventilatory support?
q.e: Above C3 damages the nerves to the respiratory muscles. C3–C5: may breathe some of the time. Below C5: may breathe but with reduced VC and weak cough.

q.q: The phrenic nerve, which drives the diaphragm, arises from which cervical levels?
q.e: "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive" — reflected in Heuer's C3/C3–C5 injury thresholds.

q.q: A patient with a C6 spinal cord injury is breathing spontaneously. What should the RT expect?
o: Reduced vital capacity and an ineffective cough
q.e: Below C5, the patient may breathe alone but has reduced VC and cannot clear secretions well. C1–C7 = tetraplegia.

q.q: A cervical SCI patient has hypotension, bradycardia, hypothermia and warm, flushed, dry skin. What type of shock is this?
q.e: Injury above T6 with bradycardia + hypothermia = neurogenic shock (vasodilation). At/below T6 with tachycardia and cold clammy skin = hemorrhagic.

q.q: On chest x-ray, phrenic nerve paralysis often shows:
o: An elevated diaphragm on the affected side
Tracheal deviation toward the unaffected side
q.e: Phrenic nerve conditions often show an elevated diaphragm, with reduced chest movement on the affected side.

q.q: An SCI patient arrives apneic. What should the RT assume and do?
o: Assume a complete high cervical injury and ventilate manually now
Wait for a C-spine x-ray to confirm the level before ventilating
Assume neurogenic shock and give IV fluids before anything else
Apply CPAP at 5 cm H₂O and reassess in 15 minutes
q.e: If apnea is present, assume complete high cervical injury and ventilate immediately, keeping the spine neutral.

sections.title: Mechanical Ventilation
sections.covers: Modes (VC, PC, IMV, MMV, SIMV, PRVC, CMV, PAV, APRV, HFOV, VV+) · phase variables · PEEP · high and low pressures · Otis equation

q.q: In Volume Control ventilation, what happens when the patient's compliance decreases?
o: VT stays the same and PIP/Pplat rise
VT falls and pressure stays the same
q.e: VC: volume is the independent (control) variable, pressure is dependent. Set Volume → Watch Pressure.

q.q: In Pressure Control ventilation, what happens when the patient develops ARDS and compliance falls?
o: Pressure stays the same and VT falls
VT stays the same and pressure rises
The ventilator switches to volume control
q.e: PC: pressure is the independent variable, volume is dependent. Set Pressure → Watch Volume (e.g., 20 cm H₂O stays 20; VT falls 500 → 300 mL).

q.q: A patient is on PC 20 cm H₂O with PEEP 10 cm H₂O. What is the PIP?
q.e: PIP = PC setting + PEEP = 20 + 10 = 30 cm H₂O.

q.q: Which flow waveform is associated with Volume Control, and which with Pressure Control?
o: VC = square (constant) flow; PC = decelerating flow
VC = decelerating flow; PC = square flow
q.e: VC: square flow, pressure "climbs like a mountain." PC: decelerating flow, pressure is a flat "table."

q.q: Which statement about VC and PC is correct?
o: Only one can be controlled — volume or pressure, not both
PC guarantees both the VT and the airway pressure
VC guarantees both the VT and the airway pressure
Both modes guarantee VT and minute ventilation
q.e: "If you control the Volume, the Pressures go up and down; if you control the Pressure, the Volumes go up and down."

q.q: When is Pressure Control preferred over Volume Control?
o: Severe ARDS, when limiting pressure matters more than a set VT
When a guaranteed minute ventilation is the top priority
In patients with normal lungs and normal compliance
When an apneic patient needs a guaranteed VT
q.e: VC is the 1st choice; PC is the 2nd choice, used when pressure limits matter more. VC pressures ≥ 50 cm H₂O cause barotrauma.

q.q: On A/C (CMV), the set rate is 10 and the patient triggers 20 breaths/min. How many breaths are fully supported mandatory breaths?
q.e: In A/C, every trigger produces a machine-cycled mandatory breath, so the patient gets 20 mandatory breaths. In CMV the mandatory rate can exceed the set rate.

q.q: On SIMV, the set rate is 10 and the patient's total rate is 20. How are the breaths delivered?
o: 10 mandatory breaths only; the patient cannot breathe in between
q.e: SIMV gives the set number of mandatory breaths; the rest are spontaneous at whatever VT the patient generates. The mandatory rate can never exceed the set rate.

q.q: A patient-triggered breath in A/C mode is classified as:
o: Mandatory, because the ventilator cycles it off
Spontaneous, because the patient triggered it
q.e: Patient-triggered ≠ spontaneous. If the ventilator controls either the start or the end, the breath is mandatory. Classic NBRC trap.

q.q: What is the main complication of A/C in an anxious patient triggering 25–35 breaths/min?
o: Diaphragm fatigue from a high workload
q.e: Every triggered breath is fully supported, so a high patient rate causes hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis.

q.q: Chang's Control mode (CMV with no patient trigger) is indicated for which patient?
o: Tetanus, seizures, or flail chest needing complete rest
A patient ready to begin weaning from the ventilator
A COPD patient with a strong spontaneous drive
A patient using BiPAP at night for sleep apnea
q.e: Control mode requires deep sedation ± paralysis. Most important alarms: low exhaled volume and low inspiratory pressure, since the patient is 100% ventilator-dependent.

q.q: How does SIMV differ from IMV?
o: SIMV times the mandatory breath to the patient's effort
SIMV allows no spontaneous breaths between mandatory ones
IMV synchronizes mandatory breaths; SIMV uses a fixed clock
SIMV guarantees the VT of every spontaneous breath
q.e: IMV delivers mandatory breaths on a rigid clock, causing breath stacking/auto-PEEP. SIMV waits for the patient's effort within a sync window.

q.q: What is the major problem with pure IMV?
o: It cannot deliver a set mandatory rate
It delivers too little minute ventilation
q.e: Mandatory breaths land on unfinished exhalations → breath stacking, auto-PEEP, ↑ airway pressures, barotrauma risk. IMV is obsolete in adult ventilators.

q.q: Why is pressure support commonly added to SIMV?
o: To reduce fatigue and work on spontaneous breaths
To increase the number of mandatory breaths
To raise the baseline pressure like PEEP
To guarantee a set VT on spontaneous breaths
q.e: Without PS, the patient must breathe through the circuit and ETT on their own spontaneous breaths → fatigue. Example: SIMV 10, VT 450, FiO₂ 30%, PS 8, PEEP 5.

q.q: In Mandatory Minute Ventilation (MMV), when are mandatory breaths delivered?
o: When measured minute ventilation falls below a set threshold
At a fixed set rate regardless of patient effort
Only after the patient is apneic for 20 seconds
Whenever the patient's rate rises above 30/min
q.e: MMV is a closed-loop IMV-type mode: the ventilator fills in only when the patient's own V̇E falls short. A weaning safety net.

q.q: How does PRVC maintain the target tidal volume?
o: It adjusts pressure each breath to hit the target VT at the lowest pressure
It delivers the same set pressure every breath and lets VT vary
It uses a fixed square-wave flow exactly like volume control
It lets the patient's own effort set the VT for every breath
q.e: PRVC is adaptive/closed-loop: compliance worsens → pressure rises; compliance improves → pressure falls. It combines VC's volume guarantee with PC's pressure limit.

q.q: Which pair of modes both guarantee tidal volume while also adjusting pressure automatically?
q.e: PRVC (mandatory breaths) and Volume Support (spontaneous, PSV with a target VT) both adapt pressure to hit a target volume.

q.q: VV+ on the Puritan Bennett 840 consists of which two modes?
q.e: VV+ = VC+ for mandatory breaths (A/C or SIMV) and Volume Support for spontaneous breaths.

q.q: In Volume Support, what happens to the pressure support level when the patient's effort increases?
o: It switches to a mandatory breath
q.e: Less patient effort → more PS; more effort → less PS, to hold the target VT. Useful for weaning.

q.q: Pressure Support Ventilation (PSV) is described as:
q.e: PSV = patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled (ends when flow falls to ~25% of peak).

q.q: Why can't PSV be used on an apneic patient?
o: Every PSV breath must be patient-triggered
It delivers too much tidal volume
It cannot be combined with PEEP
q.e: PSV is only active during spontaneous breaths. PS = help, not a breath.

q.q: To what targets is pressure support titrated?
o: PIP below 15 cm H₂O, any rate
q.e: Titrate PS to spontaneous VT 8–10 mL/kg IBW and f < 25/min.

q.q: What makes Proportional Assist Ventilation (PAV) different from PSV?
o: PAV scales pressure to the patient's effort continuously; PSV gives a fixed pressure
PAV is time-cycled at a set inspiratory time; PSV is flow-cycled at 25% of peak
PAV guarantees a set VT every breath; PSV lets the VT vary with effort
PAV is used only for apneic patients; PSV is used for spontaneous breathing
q.e: PAV is a positive-feedback servo mode. The clinician sets % support (5–95%); calculations run every 5 ms using the equation of motion.

q.q: How is VT determined in Airway Pressure-Release Ventilation (APRV)?
o: The gradient between the high pressure and the release pressure
A preset tidal volume dialed in by the clinician
The patient's own inspiratory effort alone
The oscillation amplitude around the mean pressure
q.e: APRV has two levels; VT comes from the gradient. The cycle is inverted: exhalation occurs during the pressure release.

q.q: How is a patient weaned from APRV?
o: Lower the release frequency until the patient is on CPAP
Raise the release pressure up to the high pressure
Raise the release frequency until breathing is spontaneous
Switch directly to A/C and begin an SBT
q.e: Decrease the release frequency; at zero releases the patient is on CPAP.

q.q: On HFOV, which settings control OXYGENATION?
q.e: HFOV: oxygenation = P̄aw + FiO₂. Ventilation (CO₂) = amplitude + frequency.

q.q: A patient on HFOV has a rising PaCO₂. Which change will improve ventilation?
q.e: On HFOV, lower frequency = larger VT per oscillation. Hypoventilation → ↑ amplitude or ↓ frequency; hyperventilation → ↓ amplitude or ↑ frequency.

q.q: HFOV operates at what frequency range?
q.e: HFOV delivers VT often smaller than anatomic dead space at 3–15 Hz, oscillating around a constant P̄aw.

q.q: A COPD patient has a PaCO₂ of 75 mm Hg and needs noninvasive support. Which is appropriate?
q.e: CPAP helps oxygenation but does not breathe for the patient. Hypercapnia needs IPAP (ventilation). IPAP = CO₂; EPAP = oxygenation.

q.q: CPAP is BEST described as:
o: PEEP for a spontaneously breathing patient
A mode with mandatory breaths at a set rate
Two pressure levels, IPAP and EPAP
q.e: CPAP: one continuous pressure, no mechanical breaths. The patient needs adequate drive and VT. Good for OSA, CHF, post-extubation.

q.q: What is the TRIGGER variable in mechanical ventilation?
o: What is held constant during inspiration
q.e: Trigger = start (patient or time). Limit = held constant during inspiration. Cycle = ends inspiration. Baseline = end-expiratory pressure.

q.q: What is the CYCLE variable in mechanical ventilation?
o: What is held constant during inspiration
q.e: Cycle options are volume, time or flow. VC = volume-cycled; PCV = time-cycled; PSV = flow-cycled.

q.q: Pressure Control Ventilation (PCV) is:
q.e: PCV = time-triggered (or patient), pressure-limited, time-cycled. Compare PSV = patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled.

q.q: On a pressure–time waveform, how do you identify a PATIENT-triggered breath?
o: A small negative dip below baseline before the breath
A flat baseline with no dip before the breath
A sharp pressure spike at end-inspiration
A flat plateau held during inspiration
q.e: Patient trigger = small negative deflection. Time trigger = no negative deflection.

q.q: The trigger sensitivity is set at −0.5 cm H₂O and the ventilator is delivering breaths the patient did not initiate. What is happening?
o: The patient is too weak to trigger
q.e: Too sensitive (e.g., −0.5 cm H₂O or 0.5 L/min) → auto-triggering. Too insensitive (e.g., −5) → the patient can't trigger and fatigues.

q.q: A patient has PEEP 5 cm H₂O and PIP 25 cm H₂O. What pressure is actually causing inspiration (pressure above PEEP)?
q.e: Pressure is measured above baseline: 25 − 5 = 20 cm H₂O.

q.q: In Volume Control, which is the INDEPENDENT (control) variable?
q.e: The variable the ventilator guarantees is the independent variable. VC: volume independent, pressure dependent. PC: pressure independent, volume dependent.

q.q: PEEP is BEST defined as:
o: An elevated baseline airway pressure at end-expiration
A mode of ventilation used alone
The pressure measured during an inspiratory hold
q.e: PEEP raises the end-expiratory/baseline pressure. It is applied along with another mode, not as a stand-alone mode.

q.q: What is the primary benefit of PEEP?
o: It raises FRC and recruits alveoli, reducing shunt
It lowers PaCO₂ by increasing ventilation
It increases venous return and cardiac output
It lowers ICP by improving cerebral drainage
q.e: PEEP ↑ FRC → ↑ V/Q → improves oxygenation → ↓ WOB. It is the #1 ventilator adjustment for improving oxygenation.

q.q: When should PEEP be considered for refractory hypoxemia?
o: When PaO₂/FiO₂ is below 200 mm Hg
When PaCO₂ is above 50 mm Hg
When compliance is above 100 mL/cm H₂O
q.e: Indications: intrapulmonary shunting and refractory hypoxemia (P/F < 200), decreased FRC and compliance, and auto-PEEP not responding to setting changes.

q.q: Above what PEEP level does the deck say the risk of barotrauma increases?
q.e: PEEP > 10 cm H₂O (or P̄aw > 30, or PIP > 50) is associated with an increased incidence of alveolar rupture/barotrauma.

q.q: What is the MAJOR downside of excessive PEEP?
q.e: PEEP makes pleural pressure less negative → ↓ venous return → ↓ preload → ↓ cardiac output → hypotension.

q.q: Optimal PEEP is defined as:
o: The lowest PEEP that gives the most benefit with the fewest side effects
The highest PEEP the patient can tolerate
The PEEP that produces the highest PaO₂ regardless of compliance
q.e: Titrate with PaO₂, compliance, SpO₂ and waveforms. In the deck's example, 10 was optimal because 12 lowered both PaO₂ and compliance.

q.q: PEEP is increased from 10 to 12 cm H₂O. The PaO₂ and static compliance both fall. What should the RT do?
q.e: A drop in both PaO₂ and compliance means overdistension. 10 cm H₂O was the optimal PEEP.

q.q: How does PEEP affect ICP in a head-injured patient with normal lungs?
o: It may raise ICP by impeding venous drainage
It lowers ICP by improving oxygenation
It has no effect on ICP at any level
It lowers ICP by reducing the PaCO₂
q.e: PEEP can raise ICP — most important in TBI, stroke and neurosurgical patients.

q.q: Which hemodynamic changes does PEEP cause?
q.e: Expanded alveoli compress pulmonary capillaries (↑ PVR, ↑ PAP); blood backs up (↑ CVP); ↓ CO. Also ↓ renal perfusion and urine output.

q.q: Auto-PEEP is BEST described as:
o: Gas trapped at end-expiration from incomplete exhalation
PEEP set intentionally on the ventilator by the RT
End-expiratory pressure maintained by the glottis
The pressure measured during an inspiratory hold
q.e: Auto-PEEP (intrinsic/occult) raises the baseline and makes triggering harder, increasing WOB.

q.q: A COPD patient on VC has RR 20, VT 700 mL and flow 40 L/min, with rising PIP, auto-PEEP and hypotension. Which change is appropriate?
q.e: Give the lungs more time to empty: ↑ flow (shorter I-time), ↓ VT, ↓ rate, ↑ expiratory time. Bronchodilators help in reversible obstruction.

q.q: How is auto-PEEP measured?
o: End-expiratory pause just before the next breath
End-inspiratory pause after the breath is delivered
Read the set PEEP on the ventilator display
Subtract the PEEP from the measured PIP
q.e: End-expiratory occlusion; for accuracy the patient should be sedated or paralyzed. The proximal manometer may read only the set PEEP.

q.q: When is therapeutic (applied) PEEP used for auto-PEEP?
o: After adjustments fail, to offset small-airway trapping
Before any other ventilator adjustment is made
Never — added PEEP always worsens auto-PEEP
Only when the patient is in pressure control
q.e: Therapeutic PEEP is used after adjusting flow, VT and rate — not instead of them.

q.q: The high pressure alarm sounds. Which is a likely cause?
o: Secretions or a mucus plug in the ETT
q.e: High PIP causes: secretions, kinked or bitten ETT, bronchospasm, pneumothorax, water in tubing, ↓ compliance, coughing, air trapping.

q.q: The low pressure and low exhaled volume alarms sound together. What is the MOST likely cause?
q.e: Low pressure = disconnection, circuit leak, cuff leak, loose sensor lines. The low exhaled volume alarm shares these causes.

q.q: The PIP increases from 25 to 40 cm H₂O while the Pplat stays at 20 cm H₂O. What is the MOST likely cause?
q.e: ↑ PIP with unchanged Pplat = resistance problem. "When only PIP moves, think airways."

q.q: Both PIP and Pplat rise by about 10 cm H₂O. What type of problem is this?
q.e: "When PIP and Plateau move together, think lungs." ARDS, pulmonary edema, pneumothorax, atelectasis, pneumonia, fibrosis.

q.q: Plateau pressure reflects:
o: Compliance only, measured with flow stopped
Airway resistance only, measured during flow
q.e: PIP = resistance + compliance. Pplat (no flow) = compliance only. PIP − Pplat = transairway pressure; Raw = ΔP ÷ flow.

q.q: What is the modern (ARDSNet) plateau pressure goal for lung-protective ventilation?
q.e: The notes say today's accepted goal is Pplat < 30 cm H₂O. Older Chang slides print < 35. "If you remember one ventilator pressure in ARDS, remember this one."

q.q: Which pressure is a better indicator of ventilator-induced lung injury risk, and why?
o: PEEP — it sets the baseline pressure
Mean airway pressure — it is the highest
q.e: PIP limits are historical; Pplat reflects alveolar pressure and is the better VILI indicator.

q.q: What is the ideal driving pressure (Pplat − PEEP)?
q.e: Driving pressure ΔP = Pplat − PEEP, ideally < 15 cm H₂O. PIP < 50, P̄aw < 30.

q.q: What is the normal airway resistance (Raw) in an adult?
q.e: Normal Raw ≈ 0.6–2.4 (≈1–3). Raw > 5 → airway obstruction; > 10 → severe bronchospasm, mucus plug or kinked ETT.

q.q: The high PEEP alarm sounds. What is the MOST likely cause?
q.e: High PEEP: auto-PEEP, air trapping, insufficient flow (long I-time), insufficient expiratory time. Low PEEP: circuit or cuff leak.

q.q: The apnea alarm sounds on a ventilated patient. Which is a likely cause?
q.e: Apnea/low frequency: disconnection, oversedation, prolonged neuromuscular block, respiratory center dysfunction, muscle fatigue.

q.q: When any ventilator alarm sounds, what is the correct sequence?
o: Patient → ventilator → find the cause → fix it
Silence the alarm → call the physician
Silence the alarm → widen the alarm limits
q.e: Never silence an alarm without finding the cause.

q.q: What does the Otis equation describe?
o: The respiratory rate at which work of breathing is lowest
The relationship between PaCO₂ and alveolar ventilation
The calculation of static and dynamic compliance
The PEEP level that gives the best oxygenation
q.e: Otis (Otis, Fenn & Rahn) relates rate, VT, dead space, compliance and resistance to find the rate with the least WOB. The deck flags it as absent from the decks, Heuer and Hess — look it up in Egan's.

q.q: Based on the Otis equation concept, how do patients with obstructive versus restrictive disease naturally breathe?
o: Obstructive: slow and deep. Restrictive: rapid and shallow
Obstructive: rapid and shallow. Restrictive: slow and deep
q.e: Each chooses the rate that minimizes WOB: high resistance favors slow, deep breaths; low compliance favors rapid, shallow breaths.

sections.title: BiPAP / NIPPV
sections.covers: Guidelines and goals — goals, indications, contraindications, starting settings, monitoring

q.q: What is the PRIMARY goal of BiPAP?
o: Reverse acute respiratory failure without intubating
Cure the underlying lung disease that caused failure
Provide full ventilatory support to an apneic patient
Replace the need for bronchodilators and steroids
q.e: The primary goal is to reverse acute respiratory failure WITHOUT an artificial airway. NIV will not cure the underlying disease.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT a goal of NIV therapy?
q.e: Goals: improve oxygenation and ventilation, reverse hypoxemia and acute respiratory failure, relieve distress, reverse muscle fatigue, improve mechanics, prevent/reverse atelectasis, improve compliance. NIV does not cure disease.

q.q: Which of the following IS a listed goal of NIV therapy?
o: Replace the need for ABG monitoring
q.e: Reversing respiratory muscle fatigue is a goal. NIV does not protect the airway — inability to protect the airway is a contraindication.

q.q: Which patient is an appropriate candidate for BiPAP?
o: An alert, cooperative COPD patient with moderate hypercarbia
A patient in respiratory arrest who needs rescue breathing
A hypercapnic patient with severe facial burns
An obtunded patient who cannot protect the airway
q.e: Indications include COPD exacerbation and moderate hypercarbia. The patient must be spontaneously breathing, cooperative, and able to fit and tolerate a mask.

q.q: According to the 202 deck, which is a headline indication for BiPAP?
q.e: Headline indications: prevent intubation in end-stage COPD, chronic ventilatory failure, and restrictive/neuromuscular disease and nocturnal hypoventilation.

q.q: Which set of conditions are ALL common indications for NIV?
o: Acute heart failure, OHS, post-extubation support
Cardiac arrest, respiratory arrest, facial trauma
Apnea, coma, and a massive GI bleed
q.e: Common indications: acute respiratory failure, severe hypoxemia, severe asthma, COPD exacerbation, acute heart failure, post-extubation, moderate acidemia/hypercarbia, nocturnal hypoventilation, OHS, sleep apnea.

q.q: Which is required of every patient before starting NIV?
o: Spontaneous breathing, cooperation, and mask tolerance
A PaCO₂ above 80 mm Hg on the most recent ABG
A functioning arterial line for frequent ABGs
An artificial airway already in place
q.e: The inclusion criterion layered on top of every indication: spontaneously breathing, cooperative, able to fit and tolerate a mask.

q.q: Which is a CONTRAINDICATION to BiPAP?
q.e: Contraindications: lack of cooperation, cardiac arrest, respiratory arrest, excessive secretions, inability to fit a mask, inability to protect the airway, severe facial burns or trauma.

q.q: A patient with severe facial trauma is in hypercapnic respiratory failure. What is the MOST appropriate support?
q.e: Severe facial burns or trauma is a contraindication — the mask can't work. The patient needs an artificial airway.

q.q: The contraindications to NIV fall into which two patterns?
o: The patient can't participate, or the mask can't work
The patient is too young, or too old
The PaCO₂ is too high, or too low
The patient is hypoxemic, or hypercapnic
q.e: Uncooperative, arrested, can't protect the airway = can't participate. Won't fit, burned/traumatized face, secretions = mask can't work.

q.q: Which is NOT a contraindication to BiPAP?
q.e: Moderate hypercarbia is an indication.

q.q: What are typical starting BiPAP settings?
o: IPAP 8–12 cm H₂O, EPAP 4–6 cm H₂O, backup rate 10–12
IPAP 25–30 cm H₂O, EPAP 15 cm H₂O, backup rate 20
IPAP 5 cm H₂O, EPAP 5 cm H₂O, no backup rate
IPAP 40 cm H₂O, EPAP 0 cm H₂O
q.e: Start IPAP 8–12, EPAP 4–6, BUR 10–12, plus FiO₂ and Rise.

q.q: How is the pressure support on BiPAP calculated?
q.e: PS = IPAP − EPAP, minimum 4 cm H₂O.

q.q: A patient is on IPAP 15 cm H₂O and EPAP 5 cm H₂O. What is the pressure support?
q.e: PS = 15 − 5 = 10 cm H₂O (the deck's example order: IPAP 15, EPAP 5, RR 12, FiO₂ 40%).

q.q: What is the minimum pressure support (IPAP − EPAP) on BiPAP?
q.e: PS minimum 4 cm H₂O.

q.q: In what increments are IPAP and EPAP adjusted?
q.e: Both IPAP and EPAP are adjusted in increments of 2 cm H₂O.

q.q: On BiPAP, what does a LOWER Rise setting number do?
o: Reaches the inspiratory pressure more slowly
q.e: For Rise: the lower the number, the faster the inspiratory pressure is reached.

q.q: A BiPAP patient's PaCO₂ is still elevated. Which setting change addresses ventilation?
q.e: IPAP (and the PS it creates) drives ventilation and CO₂ removal. EPAP = PEEP = oxygenation.

q.q: A BiPAP patient remains hypoxemic but the PaCO₂ is normal. Which setting change is MOST appropriate?
q.e: EPAP acts like PEEP and improves oxygenation. Raise IPAP too if you need to keep the same pressure support.

q.q: What is the IBW of a 5'6" female, and the target VT at 8 mL/kg?
What is the IBW of a 6'0" male, and the target VT at 8 mL/kg?
What defines the SUCCESSFUL application of NIV?
o: The ABG improves — PaO₂ rises and PaCO₂ falls
The patient falls asleep comfortably on the mask
q.e: The FAQ answer: overall improvement in the ABG, with PaO₂ rising and PaCO₂ falling.

q.q: A patient in respiratory failure continues to deteriorate 30 minutes after BiPAP is started. What is the BEST action?
o: Increase IPAP by 10 cm H₂O and wait another hour
q.e: If the patient continues to deteriorate ~30 minutes after NIV initiation, intubate and ventilate.

q.q: What is the acceptable Total Leak range on BiPAP?
o: 0 L/min — any leak is a problem
q.e: Total leak 7–25, never over 60. A reading of 0 or "---" is not acceptable either.

q.q: Besides the ABG, what should the RT monitor on a BiPAP patient?
o: Leak, measured VT and RR, SpO₂, and WOB
SpO₂ only, with an ABG once a day
Heart rate and blood pressure only
q.e: Watch leak trend, actual VT and RR against alarm limits, SpO₂, and WOB (which drives the Rise setting).

sections.title: Arterial Blood Gases
sections.covers: pH · PaO₂ · PaCO₂ · HCO₃⁻ · Henderson-Hasselbalch · volatile and nonvolatile acids · hydrogen ions · Severinghaus, Clark & Sanz electrodes

q.q: What is the normal arterial pH range?
q.e: Arterial pH 7.35–7.45. Venous pH is 7.30–7.40.

q.q: What is the normal arterial PaCO₂?
q.e: Arterial PaCO₂ 35–45 mm Hg. Venous PCO₂ is 42–48.

q.q: What is the normal arterial HCO₃⁻ range used on the NBRC?
q.e: The deck gives 22–28; NBRC uses 22–26 mEq/L.

q.q: What is the normal arterial PaO₂ on room air?
q.e: Arterial PaO₂ 80–100 mm Hg. Venous PO₂ is 35–45.

q.q: What is the normal venous PO₂?
q.e: Venous PO₂ is much lower (35–45) because O₂ has already been delivered to the tissues.

q.q: Why is venous PCO₂ higher than arterial PaCO₂?
o: It carries CO₂ from the tissues to the lungs
It contains more hemoglobin than arterial blood
The kidneys add CO₂ to venous blood
Venous blood has a higher pH than arterial
q.e: Venous CO₂ is higher because it is returning CO₂ from the tissues to the lungs.

q.q: What is the "perfect" ABG the deck uses for every calculation?
q.e: pH 7.40, PaCO₂ 40 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L.

q.q: When interpreting an ABG, which value do you check FIRST?
q.e: pH is the referee — it gives the direction (acidosis or alkalosis); then PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ show which system caused it.

q.q: A pH of 7.31 indicates:
q.e: pH < 7.35 = acidosis; pH > 7.45 = alkalosis.

q.q: In which patient population is a slightly acidotic pH considered NORMAL?
q.e: For a newborn ABG, slightly acidotic is normal.

q.q: PaCO₂ is the ______ component of the ABG and is controlled by the ______.
q.e: PaCO₂ = respiratory component, controlled moment-to-moment by the lungs. HCO₃⁻ = metabolic component, controlled by the kidneys.

q.q: How does PaCO₂ affect pH?
o: In the opposite direction — ↑ PaCO₂ lowers pH
In the same direction — ↑ PaCO₂ raises pH
It has no effect on pH
q.e: CO₂ + water → carbonic acid → ↓ pH. Hypoventilation → ↑ PaCO₂ → respiratory acidosis.

q.q: Which ABG value is used to judge the adequacy of VENTILATION?
q.e: PaCO₂ reflects ventilation. PaO₂ reflects oxygenation.

q.q: In an ACUTE change in PaCO₂, what does the HCO₃⁻ do initially?
o: Stays near normal — no time to compensate
Rises right away to fully compensate
Falls sharply to offset the change
q.e: Respiratory changes happen quickly; renal compensation takes 3–5 days minimum.

q.q: How does HCO₃⁻ affect pH?
o: In the same direction — ↑ HCO₃⁻ raises pH
In the opposite direction — ↑ HCO₃⁻ lowers pH
q.e: ↑ HCO₃⁻ → ↑ pH (metabolic alkalosis); ↓ HCO₃⁻ → ↓ pH (metabolic acidosis).

q.q: How long does renal compensation take?
q.e: Renal compensation is slow — 3 to 5 days minimum. A significantly elevated HCO₃⁻ suggests a chronic respiratory disorder.

q.q: A significantly elevated HCO₃⁻ should raise suspicion of:
o: Chronic compensation for a respiratory disorder
q.e: A significantly elevated HCO₃⁻ is the hallmark of chronic compensation.

q.q: Why does HCO₃⁻ fall in metabolic acidosis?
o: It is used up buffering H⁺ from fixed acids
The lungs exhale the extra bicarbonate
The bicarbonate is converted to oxygen
The kidneys stop producing hydrogen ions
q.e: H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → carbonic acid → water + CO₂. Bicarbonate is "used up" like firefighters at a bigger fire.

q.q: At what PaO₂ are the peripheral chemoreceptors stimulated to increase ventilation?
q.e: At ~60 mm Hg the peripheral chemoreceptors drive ventilation — why hypoxemia is the most common cause of acute alveolar hyperventilation.

q.q: Severe hypoxemia can add which acid-base disorder because tissues switch to anaerobic metabolism?
q.e: Anaerobic metabolism produces lactic acid, adding a metabolic acidosis — making pH and HCO₃⁻ lower than expected for the PaCO₂.

q.q: What PaO₂ is considered acceptable in a COPD patient with hypoxic drive?
q.e: In COPD, a PaO₂ around 55–60 mm Hg can be acceptable.

q.q: Which three values does a blood gas analyzer measure DIRECTLY?
q.e: Only pH, PCO₂ and PO₂ are measured. HCO₃⁻, base excess and SaO₂ are calculated.

q.q: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is used to:
o: Calculate HCO₃⁻ from the measured pH and PCO₂
Measure the PO₂ directly with an electrode
q.e: H-H mathematically links pH, the respiratory component (PCO₂) and the metabolic component (HCO₃⁻). Formula: pH = pKa + log[HCO₃⁻ ÷ (0.03 × PaCO₂)].

q.q: Which ABG value is CALCULATED rather than measured?
q.e: HCO₃⁻, BE and SaO₂ are calculated from the three measured values.

q.q: Which acid is the VOLATILE acid the lungs can eliminate?
q.e: Carbonic acid breaks down into water and CO₂, which the lungs blow off.

q.q: Nonvolatile (fixed) acids are:
o: Acids the lungs can't remove; the kidneys excrete them
Acids the lungs exhale as carbon dioxide
Only carbonic acid formed from CO₂ and water
Bases that raise the pH when they accumulate
q.e: Fixed acids must be buffered by bicarbonate and excreted by the kidneys.

q.q: Which is an example of a NONVOLATILE (fixed) acid?
q.e: Fixed acids: lactic acid, keto acids (DKA), salicylate acids, and phosphoric and sulfuric acids from catabolism.

q.q: When fixed acids accumulate, what happens to the HCO₃⁻ and the anion gap?
o: HCO₃⁻ falls and the anion gap rises
HCO₃⁻ rises and the anion gap falls
q.e: Fixed acids release H⁺, which consumes HCO₃⁻ and raises the anion gap.

q.q: What is the relationship between hydrogen ion concentration and pH?
o: Inverse — more H⁺ means a lower pH
Direct — more H⁺ means a higher pH
Logarithmic but in the same direction
q.e: pH = −log[H⁺]. More free H⁺ = lower pH = more acidic.

q.q: A normal blood pH of 7.40 corresponds to an [H⁺] of about:
q.e: Hess: pH 7.4 corresponds to [H⁺] of 40 nmol/L. pH 7.0 = 100 nmol/L.

q.q: Which process causes metabolic alkalosis through loss of H⁺?
q.e: Losing H⁺ (vomiting, gastric suction, hypokalemia shift, steroids/aldosterone) raises the pH.

q.q: Which electrode measures PCO₂?
q.e: Severinghaus = PCO₂. Clark = PO₂. Sanz = pH.

q.q: Which electrode measures PO₂?
q.e: Clark is polarographic: O₂ is reduced at a cathode, producing a current proportional to the O₂ present.

q.q: Which electrode measures pH?
q.e: Sanz is a glass electrode sensitive to hydrogen ions.

q.q: How does the Severinghaus electrode work?
o: CO₂ changes a solution's pH, which is read as PCO₂
O₂ is reduced at a cathode, producing a current
A glass membrane responds directly to H⁺
Light absorption by hemoglobin is measured
q.e: Severinghaus reads PCO₂ through a pH change caused by CO₂ diffusion.

q.q: Which electrode uses a polarographic method in which oxygen is reduced at a cathode?
q.e: Clark = polarographic O₂ electrode.

q.q: ABG: pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 58 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 25 mEq/L. Interpret.
q.e: pH low, PaCO₂ high, HCO₃⁻ normal → acute ventilatory failure (pH < 7.35 with PaCO₂ > 45).

q.q: ABG: pH 7.52, PaCO₂ 28 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 23 mEq/L. Interpret.
q.e: pH high, PaCO₂ low, HCO₃⁻ normal → acute alveolar hyperventilation (pH > 7.45 with PaCO₂ < 35).

q.q: ABG: pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 40 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 16 mEq/L. Interpret.
q.e: pH low with a low HCO₃⁻ and normal PaCO₂ → metabolic acidosis.

q.q: ABG: pH 7.50, PaCO₂ 41 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 32 mEq/L. Interpret.
q.e: pH high with a high HCO₃⁻ and normal PaCO₂ → metabolic alkalosis (e.g., vomiting, gastric suction).

sections.title: Asthma
sections.covers: Epidemiology · pathophysiology · risk factors · phenotypes · severity classifications and steps · SABA, LABA and controllers · peak flow meters · indications for mechanical ventilation

q.q: About how many people in the United States have asthma?
q.e: CDC: ~25 million (18.4 million adults, 6.2 million children). Worldwide (WHO): ~235 million.

q.q: How does asthma prevalence by sex change with age?
o: More common in boys in childhood; more common in women after puberty
More common in girls in childhood; more common in men after puberty
q.e: Boys > girls in childhood; the pattern flips after puberty, so women > men in adults.

q.q: According to the WHO, asthma is:
o: The most common chronic disease among children worldwide
Rare in low- and middle-income countries
More common in adults than children worldwide
q.e: Asthma is the most common chronic disease among children worldwide; >80% of asthma deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries.

q.q: What are the three headline pathologic changes in asthma?
o: Alveolar destruction, loss of elastic recoil, and bullae formation
Pulmonary fibrosis, restriction, and reduced lung volumes
Pleural effusion, atelectasis, and lobar consolidation
q.e: The three hallmarks: reversible bronchoconstriction, inflammation, and increased airway hyperresponsiveness.

q.q: Which cell type infiltrates the bronchial mucosa in asthma, and what crystals form from its breakdown?
q.e: Eosinophils infiltrate the mucosa; Charcot-Leyden crystals come from eosinophil breakdown in allergic asthma.

q.q: Why can mucus plugs cause atelectasis in asthma?
o: Goblet cell hyperplasia and big mucous glands make thick plugs
Surfactant production increases and floods the small airways
Alveolar walls are destroyed and the air spaces collapse
The diaphragm weakens and cannot expand the lower lobes
q.e: Goblet cell hyperplasia and enlarged glands produce thick, tenacious mucus → plugs → atelectasis. Functionally there is air trapping and hyperinflation.

q.q: In extrinsic (allergic) asthma, which antibody attaches to mast cells during sensitization?
q.e: First exposure → IgE production → IgE attaches to mast cells. Re-exposure → mast cell degranulation.

q.q: Which mediators are released when mast cells degranulate?
q.e: These cause bronchoconstriction, mucus hypersecretion, and increased vascular permeability → airway edema.

q.q: How long does the EARLY phase of an asthmatic response last?
o: Starts within minutes; resolves in about 1 hour
Starts hours later; lasts for several days
Starts after 24 hours; lasts about a week
Starts within minutes; lasts about 24 hours
q.e: Early phase: minutes, resolves ~1 hr. Late phase: starts hours later with eosinophils, basophils, neutrophils and T-cells, and lasts longer. Both = biphasic.

q.q: Airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) is measured with:
q.e: AHR is an exaggerated bronchoconstrictor response to many stimuli (exercise, cold air, irritants, infections), measured by bronchoprovocation (methacholine challenge).

q.q: What is the long-term consequence of airway remodeling in asthma?
o: Complete reversal of all airway obstruction
A large increase in lung compliance
q.e: Remodeling: thickened walls, more smooth muscle, fibrosis, thickened basement membrane. If it progresses, obstruction becomes partially irreversible.
