q.q: Which HOST factor is associated with worse asthma control and reduced response to therapy?
q.e: Host factors: genetics/family history, sex differences, and obesity.

q.q: Which viral infections are listed as environmental asthma triggers?
q.e: Environmental triggers: pollution, tobacco smoke, occupational exposures, viral infections (RSV, rhinovirus), and diet.

q.q: Why do beta-blockers worsen asthma?
o: They block the β₂ receptors that cause bronchodilation
They stimulate mast cells to release histamine
They increase IgE production after allergen exposure
They cause GERD, which triggers bronchospasm
q.e: Beta-blockers block β₂-mediated bronchodilation. Aspirin and NSAIDs can also trigger bronchospasm.

q.q: Which food additives can provoke an asthma attack?
q.e: Sulfites (dried fruit, shrimp, beer, wine) and the dye tartrazine.

q.q: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction is worse in which conditions?
q.e: It is worse in cold air and thought to come from cooling and drying of the airways.

q.q: Which asthma phenotype typically begins in childhood, has eosinophilic inflammation, and responds WELL to ICS?
q.e: Allergic asthma: childhood onset, family history of atopy, eosinophilic, responds well to ICS.

q.q: Which asthma phenotype typically starts in adulthood (often women), is nonallergic, and is often corticosteroid-resistant?
q.e: Late-onset asthma needs higher ICS doses and can be corticosteroid-resistant.

q.q: Which phenotype features prominent symptoms with minimal eosinophilia and a BMI over 30?
q.e: Asthma with obesity: prominent symptoms, minimal eosinophilia, harder to control.

q.q: Asthma with fixed airflow limitation is caused by:
o: An acute viral infection of the airways
q.e: Long-standing asthma → remodeling → persistent obstruction that is not fully reversible.

q.q: How does INTRINSIC asthma differ from EXTRINSIC asthma?
o: Intrinsic: no allergen link, normal IgE, adult onset
Intrinsic: high IgE and onset in early childhood
Intrinsic: triggered only by pollen and dust mites
Intrinsic: always responds to allergy injections
q.e: Extrinsic: allergen-triggered, atopy, ↑ IgE, children/young adults. Intrinsic: nonspecific triggers (infection, exercise, cold air, stress, GERD), normal IgE, adult onset.

q.q: An asthmatic speaks in single words, sits upright, has RR > 30 and a PEFR < 50% predicted. What is the exacerbation severity?
q.e: Severe: breathless at rest, single words, RR often > 30, marked retractions, PEFR < 50%, SaO₂ < 92%, pulsus paradoxus > 25 mm Hg.

q.q: What is the PEFR in a MODERATE asthma exacerbation?
q.e: Mild ≥ 80%; moderate 50–80%; severe < 50%.

q.q: What SaO₂ defines a SEVERE asthma exacerbation?
q.e: Mild > 95%; moderate 92–95%; severe < 92%.

q.q: During a severe asthma attack, the wheezing suddenly disappears and the patient becomes drowsy. What does this mean?
o: Arrest is imminent — airflow has nearly stopped
The patient is resting comfortably from relief
The exacerbation has improved to mild
q.e: A silent chest is never improvement. Drowsiness, silent chest, paradoxical movement, bradycardia and rising PaCO₂ = arrest imminent.

q.q: In a MILD asthma exacerbation, the wheeze is typically:
q.e: Mild: expiratory only. Moderate: throughout expiration ± inspiratory. Severe: biphasic. Arrest imminent: silent.

q.q: Loss of pulsus paradoxus in a severe asthmatic indicates:
o: Muscle fatigue — arrest may be imminent
A normal finding in severe asthma
q.e: Pulsus paradoxus > 25 mm Hg in severe; its loss signals muscle fatigue and imminent arrest.

q.q: When should asthma therapy be stepped DOWN?
o: After at least 3 months of stable control
q.e: Stepwise approach: step up for poor control; step down after ≥ 3 months of stable control.

q.q: Step 2 care corresponds to which chronic severity category?
q.e: Step 2 = mild persistent asthma. Cromolyn and antileukotrienes are alternatives to ICS at Step 2.

q.q: Which Step 2 alternative to ICS is preferred in infants and young children because of ICS safety concerns?
q.e: Cromolyn is preferred in infants and young children needing Step 2 care.

q.q: Monoclonal antibodies (biologics) are reserved for which asthma patients?
o: Severe persistent asthma uncontrolled on ICS + LABA
Intermittent asthma needing only a rescue inhaler
Mild persistent asthma as the first-line controller
Acute exacerbations treated in the emergency department
q.e: Biologics are add-ons when ICS + LABA is not enough.

q.q: What is the key difference between reliever and controller medications?
o: Relievers open airways now; controllers suppress inflammation daily
Controllers open airways during attacks; relievers are taken daily
Both types treat inflammation and bronchospasm equally
Relievers are taken orally; controllers are always inhaled
q.e: Relievers (rescue) = acute bronchodilation. Controllers = daily anti-inflammatory; they do nothing for an acute attack.

q.q: Which drug is a SABA (short-acting β-agonist)?
q.e: SABAs: albuterol, levalbuterol. Salmeterol = LABA; fluticasone = ICS; montelukast = leukotriene modifier.

q.q: What is the onset and duration of albuterol (SABA)?
q.e: SABA: onset 15 min, peak 30–60 min, duration 4–6 hr.

q.q: Which rule applies to LABAs in asthma?
o: Never use a LABA alone — pair it with an ICS
LABAs are the first-line rescue medication
LABAs replace ICS in mild persistent asthma
LABAs are safe as monotherapy in children
q.e: LABAs must always be paired with an ICS; children must use a LABA with a corticosteroid.

q.q: Which is a LABA?
q.e: LABAs: salmeterol, formoterol, arformoterol, indacaterol, olodaterol, vilanterol.

q.q: Salmeterol (Serevent) has what onset and duration?
q.e: Salmeterol: DPI only, onset 20 min (slower than albuterol), peak 3–5 hr, duration 12 hr.

q.q: Which LABA has a fast (about 3-minute) onset?
q.e: Formoterol: β₂-selective, 3-min onset, up to 12 hr.

q.q: What is the first-line controller (foundation) for long-term asthma control?
q.e: ICS (beclomethasone, budesonide, fluticasone, ciclesonide, mometasone) is the foundation of long-term control.

q.q: What should a patient do after using an inhaled corticosteroid?
o: Rinse the mouth to prevent oral thrush
q.e: Long-term ICS can cause oral thrush; rinse the mouth after use.

q.q: Which combination product contains an ICS and a LABA?
q.e: ICS + LABA: Advair, Symbicort, Dulera, Breo. DuoNeb is SABA + SAMA.

q.q: How does cromolyn sodium work, and when is it used?
o: Relaxes smooth muscle — for acute attacks
q.e: Mast cell stabilizer; prophylactic only; takes 2–4 weeks to show improvement.

q.q: Montelukast (Singulair) is classified as:
q.e: Leukotriene modifiers: montelukast and zafirlukast (receptor blockers), zileuton (5-lipoxygenase inhibitor). Oral controllers, not for acute attacks.

q.q: Which leukotriene modifier inhibits 5-lipoxygenase and requires liver function monitoring?
q.e: Zileuton (Zyflo), 600 mg QID; caution with theophylline and warfarin.

q.q: Omalizumab (Xolair) works by:
o: Blocking IgE binding to mast cells
q.e: Omalizumab = anti-IgE (allergic asthma). Benralizumab, mepolizumab, reslizumab block IL-5. Most severe risk: anaphylaxis.

q.q: Levalbuterol (Xopenex) is:
q.e: The R-isomer does the bronchodilating; the S-isomer is ~100× less potent and may worsen airway responsiveness.

q.q: While giving albuterol, the RT should stop and notify if the heart rate increases by:
q.e: Tachycardia threshold: 20 bpm or 20% increase. Other side effects: tremor, palpitations, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, paradoxical bronchospasm.

q.q: Which is a known side effect of β-agonists like albuterol?
q.e: β-agonist side effects: tremor, tachycardia, palpitations, headache, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia. Thrush is from ICS.

q.q: Which drug is used mainly for upper-airway swelling (croup, post-extubation stridor) rather than routine asthma?
q.e: Racemic epinephrine: ultra-short acting (onset 3–5 min, < 3 hr), mucosal vasoconstriction.

q.q: A patient's peak flow is 65% of personal best. Which action plan zone is this?
q.e: Green 80–100%; Yellow 50–80%; Red < 50%.

q.q: A patient in the GREEN zone (80–100% of personal best) should:
q.e: Green = well controlled; continue controllers.

q.q: A patient's peak flow is 40% of personal best. What should they do?
o: Use rescue medication now; call the provider urgently
Continue the usual controller and recheck tomorrow
Increase activity to open the airways
Wait 24 hours and recheck the peak flow
q.e: Red zone (< 50%): rescue medication now, systemic therapy if prescribed, urgent provider contact. Cyanosis or inability to talk = call 911.

q.q: Peak flow zones are scored against:
q.e: Zones use the patient's personal best.

q.q: Which peak flow finding supports a diagnosis of asthma?
o: A constant value every day for a week
q.e: Daily variability > 10% in adults (> 13% in children) or PEFR improvement ≥ 20% after anti-inflammatory therapy.

q.q: A status asthmaticus patient's ABG goes from pH 7.50 / PaCO₂ 30 to pH 7.38 / PaCO₂ 42 over two hours, and the patient looks tired. What does this indicate?
o: The patient is tiring — failure is near
The patient is improving with treatment
q.e: Moving from respiratory alkalosis to a normal or rising PaCO₂ is the red flag for impending failure.

q.q: Which findings indicate the need for intubation and mechanical ventilation in status asthmaticus?
o: Expiratory wheeze with a normal ABG
q.e: The MV protocol is indicated in acute ventilatory failure: fatigue, ↑ PaCO₂, ↓ pH, ↓ PaO₂.

q.q: Continuous nebulized albuterol for a severe adult asthmatic is generally given at what dose, and why?
q.e: Continuous albuterol ~10–15 mg/hr in adults, used to try to avoid respiratory failure and intubation. Adjuncts: heliox, magnesium sulfate, SQ epinephrine.

sections.title: COPD
sections.covers: Definition · diagnosis · symptoms · etiology · pathophysiology · nonpulmonary consequences and cachexia · risk factors · LTOT

q.q: Which statement BEST defines COPD?
o: A preventable, treatable, progressive, irreversible airflow limitation
A fully reversible airflow obstruction caused by allergen exposure
A restrictive disease caused by fibrosis of the lung tissue
An acute infection of the lower airways and alveoli
q.e: COPD is preventable and treatable, but once it starts the airflow limitation is irreversible and progressive. Cigarette smoke is the most common cause.

q.q: How does COPD affect lung compliance and elastic recoil?
o: Increases compliance and decreases elastic recoil
Decreases compliance and increases elastic recoil
q.e: Key terms: chronic ventilatory failure, chronic hypercapnia, INCREASED lung compliance, DECREASED elastic recoil, chronic CO₂ retention.

q.q: What are the four classic symptoms of COPD?
o: Dyspnea, chronic cough, sputum production and wheezing
Fever, chills, night sweats and weight gain
Chest pain, palpitations, syncope and edema
q.e: Dyspnea (especially on exertion), chronic cough, sputum and wheezing. These raise suspicion but are not diagnostic by themselves.

q.q: What spirometry result CONFIRMS a diagnosis of COPD?
q.e: COPD is confirmed only by spirometry: post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC < 0.70 — the obstruction does not go away after a bronchodilator.

q.q: Why is "post-bronchodilator" the key word in the COPD diagnostic criterion?
o: It proves the obstruction persists after bronchodilation
It ensures the patient's FVC is at its maximum
It rules out a restrictive lung disease
It allows the DLCO to be measured accurately
q.e: Persistent obstruction after bronchodilation = irreversible airflow limitation = COPD.

q.q: Why does the FEV₁/FVC ratio fall in COPD?
o: Obstruction slows exhalation, so FEV₁ drops more
FVC drops more than FEV₁ as the lungs stiffen
Both FEV₁ and FVC rise with hyperinflation
Restriction lowers the FVC more than the FEV₁
q.e: A normal person exhales 80–85% of FVC in the first second; the example COPD spirogram shows ~66%.

q.q: Which patient should be considered for COPD per GOLD?
o: A 55-year-old smoker with chronic cough and dyspnea
A 30-year-old never-smoker with a sprained ankle
A 20-year-old with a single episode of pneumonia
q.e: GOLD: consider COPD in patients over 40 with dyspnea, chronic cough or sputum, smoking or risk-factor exposure, or a family history of COPD.

q.q: What does GOLD stand for?
o: Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease
q.e: GOLD is an international expert committee that publishes the worldwide standard of care for COPD.

q.q: About how many people in the United States have chronic bronchitis, emphysema, or both?
q.e: 10–15 million, and most authorities agree COPD is underdiagnosed.

q.q: Why is COPD considered underdiagnosed?
o: Patients blame early symptoms on aging
It causes no symptoms at any stage
It can only be diagnosed at autopsy
q.e: Patients attribute early symptoms to aging.

q.q: What is the current gender pattern of COPD?
o: Five times more common in men
q.e: Historically more common in men because of smoking rates; now roughly equal, and women's lungs may be more susceptible.

q.q: In COPD, what happens to the distal airways during expiration, and why?
o: They collapse from lost recoil and support
They fill with fluid and secretions
They stay the same throughout exhalation
q.e: Loss of recoil and small-airway support → collapse during expiration → air trapping, hyperinflation, barrel chest.

q.q: Why do patients with advanced COPD develop chronic CO₂ retention?
o: WOB is so high the body accepts an easier, less effective pattern
The kidneys stop excreting CO₂ as the disease progresses
The patient hyperventilates, which raises the PaCO₂
Surfactant production rises and blocks CO₂ diffusion
q.e: The patient spends more O₂ breathing than they gain, so the body accepts CO₂ retention.

q.q: How is CHRONIC BRONCHITIS defined?
o: Productive cough ≥ 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years
Permanent enlargement of air spaces past the terminal bronchioles
A post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC below 0.70 on spirometry
Wheezing that fully reverses after a dose of albuterol
q.e: Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically (cough ≥ 3 months × 2 consecutive years). Emphysema is defined pathologically.

q.q: How is EMPHYSEMA defined?
o: Permanent enlargement and destruction of air spaces distal to terminal bronchioles
A productive cough for 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years
Reversible airway obstruction that improves after a bronchodilator
Fibrosis and thickening of the alveolar walls with reduced volumes
q.e: Emphysema is defined pathologically.

q.q: A stocky, cyanotic COPD patient has a chronic productive cough and peripheral edema. Which type is dominant?
q.e: Blue = cyanosis from hypoxemia; Bloater = fluid retention from cor pulmonale.

q.q: A thin, cachectic COPD patient with a barrel chest breathes through pursed lips and has little sputum. Which type is dominant?
q.e: Pink = oxygenation preserved early; Puffer = pursed-lip breathing.

q.q: Which finding is expected in EMPHYSEMA but not chronic bronchitis?
q.e: Emphysema destroys the alveolar-capillary membrane → ↓ DLCO. In chronic bronchitis DLCO is typically normal.

q.q: Percussion over the chest of an emphysema patient is typically:
q.e: Emphysema: hyperresonant, decreased breath sounds. Chronic bronchitis: normal percussion, wheezes and crackles.

q.q: Why is polycythemia common in the Blue Bloater?
q.e: Chronic hypoxemia → ↑ erythropoietin → polycythemia.

q.q: Which chest x-ray finding is typical of emphysema?
o: Hyperinflation, flat diaphragm, and blebs or bullae
q.e: Emphysema: hyperinflation, flat diaphragm, blebs/bullae. Chronic bronchitis: ↑ bronchovascular markings, cardiomegaly.

q.q: Why do chronic CO₂ retainers develop low chloride (hypochloremia)?
o: Kidneys retain HCO₃⁻, so Cl⁻ falls
Chloride is lost in the sputum
Diuretics add chloride to the blood
q.e: As HCO₃⁻ rises, Cl⁻ falls. Hypernatremia follows from aldosterone/ADH stimulation.

q.q: Which organisms are typical in the sputum of a chronic bronchitis patient?
o: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis
q.e: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis. Emphysema cultures are usually normal (minimal sputum).

q.q: What does "cachectic" mean?
o: Wasted and underweight from chronic illness
q.e: Cachexia (kuh-KEK-tik) is disease-driven wasting, not simply being thin.

q.q: Why do emphysema patients become cachectic?
o: The energy cost of breathing causes weight loss
Fluid retention hides their true weight
q.e: Significant energy expenditure on breathing → weight loss, thin appearance, muscle wasting. Nutrition is part of COPD treatment.

q.q: Which of the following is a NONPULMONARY consequence of COPD?
q.e: Nonpulmonary: cachexia, cor pulmonale (edema, JVD, cardiomegaly), polycythemia, electrolyte changes, clubbing, cyanosis.

q.q: A COPD patient has pedal edema, JVD and cardiomegaly. What is the cause?
o: Left heart failure from an MI
q.e: Chronic hypoxemia → pulmonary vasoconstriction → pulmonary hypertension → right heart failure.

q.q: Having COPD increases a patient's risk of:
q.e: The deck names increased risk of heart disease, lung cancer, cor pulmonale, acute-on-chronic failure and recurrent exacerbations.

q.q: What is the best predictor of a future COPD exacerbation?
q.e: Exacerbation risk is self-reinforcing and rises significantly in GOLD 3 and 4.

q.q: Which vaccinations are recommended for COPD patients to reduce exacerbations?
q.e: Respiratory infections are a major exacerbation trigger, so flu, pneumococcal and Tdap vaccines matter.

q.q: What is the BIGGEST contributor to developing COPD?
q.e: Tobacco smoke is the biggest contributor. Others: biomass smoke, occupational dust/fumes, air pollution.

q.q: Which GENETIC condition is a risk factor for developing COPD?
q.e: AAT deficiency is the genetic predisposition named in the deck.

q.q: Which is an additional risk factor for DEVELOPING COPD?
q.e: Others: impaired lung growth, low socioeconomic status, asthma/bronchial hyperreactivity, chronic bronchitis, tuberculosis, age.

q.q: Biomass smoke from cooking and heating is a risk factor for COPD because it is:
q.e: Exposure to particles: tobacco, biomass smoke, occupational dust and chemicals, air pollution.

q.q: What room-air values qualify a COPD patient for continuous long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT)?
q.e: LTOT threshold: SaO₂ ≤ 88% OR PaO₂ ≤ 55 torr on room air — meeting either qualifies.

q.q: A COPD patient on room air has PaO₂ 54 torr and SaO₂ 87%. Does the patient qualify for LTOT?
o: Yes — both values meet the criteria
q.e: PaO₂ ≤ 55 or SaO₂ ≤ 88% qualifies.

q.q: A COPD patient on room air has PaO₂ 62 torr and SaO₂ 91%. Does the patient qualify for continuous LTOT?
o: No — neither value meets the threshold
q.e: Neither PaO₂ ≤ 55 nor SaO₂ ≤ 88% is met.

q.q: When does Medicare reimburse NOCTURNAL oxygen therapy?
o: SpO₂ drop > 5% or SpO₂ < 88%, plus symptoms
Any snoring reported by a bed partner
SpO₂ below 95% at any time during sleep
PaO₂ below 80 mm Hg on a night-time ABG
q.e: > 5% drop or SpO₂ < 88%, plus symptoms (impaired cognition, insomnia) — basically the same as continuous LTOT criteria.

sections.title: Airway Management
sections.covers: ETT sizes and cuff pressures · Mallampati · induction agents · ETT and VAP reduction · etomidate, ketamine, midazolam, propofol · OPA vs NPA · oral vs nasal intubation

q.q: What ETT size (internal diameter) is typically used for an adult female?
q.e: Adult women 7–7.5 mm ID; adult men 8–8.5 mm ID.

q.q: What ETT size (internal diameter) is typically used for an adult male?
q.e: Adult men 8–8.5 mm ID.

q.q: Using Hess's formula, what size ETT is estimated for a 4-year-old child?
q.e: ETT size (mm ID) = (age ÷ 4) + 4 = (4 ÷ 4) + 4 = 5.0 mm. Have a half-size larger and smaller available.

q.q: Using Hess's formula, what size ETT is estimated for an 8-year-old child?
What is the narrowest part of the airway in an adult, and in a child (NBRC answer)?
o: Adult = glottis (vocal cords); child = cricoid ring
q.e: Adult trachea is cylindrical with the glottis narrowest; the pediatric airway is funnel-shaped with the cricoid narrowest.

q.q: Why is 1 mm of airway edema more dangerous in an infant than an adult?
o: It can cut the airway diameter by over 50%
Infants have wider airways than adults
q.e: The infant airway is so small that 1 mm of circumferential edema can cut the diameter by more than half.

q.q: Which laryngoscope blade lifts the epiglottis DIRECTLY?
q.e: Miller (straight) lifts the epiglottis directly. Macintosh (curved) sits in the vallecula and lifts it indirectly.

q.q: When a cuffed ETT is used in a child, what cuff pressure limit does Hess give?
q.e: Pediatric cuffs: keep below 20 cm H₂O — lower than the adult 20–30 cm H₂O target.

q.q: How does Hess estimate ETT insertion depth (at the lips) in an infant?
q.e: Infant depth = weight (kg) + 6 cm, measured from the lips.

q.q: What is the recommended adult ETT cuff pressure?
q.e: 20–30 cm H₂O — the single most testable number in the airway deck.

q.q: Why should cuff pressure stay BELOW 30 cm H₂O?
o: It can compress tracheal capillaries, causing ischemia
It allows microaspiration past the cuff
It lowers the peak inspiratory pressure
It causes the cuff to deflate over time
q.e: Tracheal capillary perfusion pressure is 25–35 mm Hg; above 30 cm H₂O risks mucosal ischemia.

q.q: Why should cuff pressure stay ABOVE 20 cm H₂O?
o: Microaspiration past the cuff becomes likely
q.e: Low cuff pressure → microaspiration → VAP.

q.q: A cuff pressure of 45 cm H₂O is needed to seal the airway. What is the most likely cause?
o: The tube is too small or malpositioned
The tube is too large for the trachea
q.e: Causes of high cuff pressure: a tube that is too small and incorrect ETT positioning.

q.q: Which type of cuff is used on most ETTs today?
q.e: High tracheal wall pressures injure mucosa, so most cuffs are high-volume, low-pressure.

q.q: Describe the Minimal Occlusion Volume (MOV) technique.
o: Inflate until no leak is heard at end-inspiration
Inflate until a slight leak is heard at end-inspiration
Inflate with exactly 10 mL of air every time
Inflate until the pilot balloon feels firm
q.e: MOV: stethoscope on the trachea, inflate until no leak at end-inspiration (when the trachea is widest).

q.q: Describe the Minimal Leak Technique (MLT).
o: Seal the cuff, then withdraw air until a slight end-inspiratory leak
Inflate until no leak is heard at end-inspiration
Inflate to 40 cm H₂O and leave it there
Leave the cuff deflated during ventilation
q.e: MLT: seal, then withdraw a little air to a slight end-inspiratory leak. MOV is generally preferred.

q.q: What does the Mallampati classification assess?
o: Oropharynx visibility to predict intubation difficulty
Neck circumference to predict sleep apnea
Degree of airway edema after extubation
q.e: Patient opens the mouth widely and extends the tongue; higher class = harder intubation.

q.q: Mallampati Class I shows which structures?
o: Soft palate and part of the uvula
q.e: Class I = all structures visible; easiest airway.

q.q: Mallampati Class IV shows which structures?
o: Soft palate, uvula, fauces and pillars
Soft palate and part of the uvula
q.e: Class IV = hard palate only; most difficult airway, also linked to sleep apnea.

q.q: Mallampati Class III shows:
o: Only the soft palate; the uvula is mostly hidden
Soft palate, uvula, fauces and pillars
Soft palate and part of the uvula
q.e: Class III = soft palate only → potentially difficult airway.

q.q: A Mallampati score of 3 or 4 also suggests increased risk of:
q.e: Mallampati 3–4 suggests anatomical narrowing and predicts ↑ OSA risk.

q.q: Which bedside finding predicts a potentially difficult airway?
q.e: Also: macroglossia, neck mass, anterior larynx, decreased mandibular space, reduced mouth opening, dental overbite.

q.q: What are induction agents?
o: IV anesthetics used to induce RSI
q.e: Induction Agents = Anesthetic Meds (word play). Etomidate, ketamine, midazolam and propofol are all induction agents.

q.q: A hypotensive trauma patient needs intubation. Which induction agent is the hemodynamically STABLE choice?
q.e: Etomidate won't drop the pressure — use it in the unstable patient. Ketamine is also tolerated in hypotension.

q.q: Which induction agent is a good choice for a patient in severe bronchospasm or who is hypotensive?
q.e: Ketamine is good in hypotension or bronchospasm.

q.q: Which induction agent has rapid onset and short duration but can cause HYPOTENSION?
q.e: Propofol: fast on, fast off; used with a paralytic; can cause hypotension.

q.q: Midazolam is classified as a:
q.e: Midazolam is a benzodiazepine; its slower onset makes it less ideal when seconds matter.

q.q: Ketamine's limitation — vivid, disturbing dreams on awakening — is called:
q.e: Emergence phenomenon (reaction/delirium). Hess: uncommon after a single induction dose.

q.q: How does a subglottic secretion drainage (SSD) ETT reduce VAP?
o: It suctions secretions pooled above the cuff
It has no cuff, so nothing pools
It delivers antibiotics directly to the lungs
It is inserted nasally to avoid the mouth
q.e: SSD tubes (Hi-Lo Evac, SealGuard, TaperGuard) remove pooled subglottic secretions.

q.q: Which ETT feature has shown reduced VAP in clinical trials?
q.e: Silver- and antibiotic-coated ETTs have shown reduced VAP; SSD tubes too.

q.q: What is the caveat about SSD tubes?
o: Less VAP, but no mortality benefit and frequent failure
More VAP because of the extra suction lumen
q.e: The benefit may come from their ultrathin polyurethane cuffs rather than the suction lumen.

q.q: Why should routine NASAL intubation be avoided in terms of VAP?
o: It causes sinusitis, raising VAE risk
q.e: Nasal intubation → sinusitis → increased VAE risk.

q.q: An oropharyngeal airway (OPA) should be used ONLY in which patients?
o: Unconscious patients without a gag reflex
Semi-comatose patients with a gag reflex
Patients with a basilar skull fracture only
q.e: An OPA requires absence of a gag reflex; it must NOT be used in semi-comatose or alert patients.

q.q: A patient does not arouse but still coughs and gags. Which airway adjunct is appropriate?
q.e: The NPA is for the patient who doesn't arouse but still has a gag/cough — the deck's own Stop-and-Think answer.

q.q: What happens if an OPA is TOO LARGE?
o: It pushes the epiglottis against the pharynx
It pushes the tongue against the pharynx
It slides harmlessly into the esophagus
It has no effect on the airway
q.e: Too large → epiglottis pushed against the pharynx/larynx. Too small → tongue pushed back. Both obstruct.

q.q: An NPA is contraindicated in a patient with which injury?
q.e: Hess: with a basilar skull fracture, an NPA may enter the cranial vault.

q.q: What are the major complications of an NPA?
o: Broken teeth if the patient bites down
q.e: Use with caution in low platelet counts or anticoagulation (bleeding).

q.q: What is the major risk of an OPA?
q.e: OPA risks: regurgitation and aspiration (major), and broken teeth if the patient bites down.

q.q: What is used to lubricate an NPA before insertion?
q.e: Lubricate with water-soluble gel, then insert along the floor of the nose parallel to the hard palate.

q.q: When is NASOTRACHEAL intubation indicated?
o: No mouth access — trismus, oral trauma
When a larger ETT is needed
q.e: Nasal intubation: no mouth access (trauma surgery), trismus, oral trauma/deformity, mandible fracture, short neck.

q.q: Which piece of equipment is REQUIRED for nasal intubation but not oral?
q.e: Magill forceps are required for nasal intubation; a stylet is NOT used.

q.q: What is a disadvantage of nasal intubation compared with oral?
o: It is less well tolerated than oral
It causes more gagging than oral
q.e: Nasal: better tolerated with potentially less tracheal injury, but smaller tube → higher resistance, harder to insert, sinusitis.

q.q: What is an advantage of nasal intubation over oral intubation?
q.e: Nasal intubation is better tolerated with potential for less tracheal injury.

q.q: Why is a bite block used with ORAL intubation?
o: So the patient can't bite the tube
To hold the stylet in place
q.e: A bite block keeps the patient from occluding the ETT by biting. A stylet is optional for oral intubation.

sections.title: Ventilation vs. Oxygenation
sections.covers: Definitions and differences · calculating VT · oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve and shifts · dead space · CO poisoning

q.q: Which ABG value reflects VENTILATION, and which reflects OXYGENATION?
q.e: Ventilation = CO₂ = PaCO₂. Oxygenation = O₂ = PaO₂. Acid-base = pH.

q.q: How does the deck define VENTILATORY failure?
q.e: Ventilatory failure = hypoventilation → ↑ PaCO₂ (> 45) with pH < 7.35 (respiratory acidosis).

q.q: How does the deck define OXYGENATION failure?
o: PaO₂ < 80 mm Hg on room air
q.e: Oxygenation failure = PaO₂ < 40 mm Hg in spite of FiO₂ 50–100%.

q.q: An opioid overdose patient has pH 7.14, PaCO₂ 105 mm Hg, PaO₂ 36 mm Hg. What is the PRIMARY problem?
o: Oxygenation only — the lungs are shunting
q.e: The deck's worked example: a ventilation problem first. Fix the ventilation and the PaO₂ will follow.

q.q: A patient with ARDS has a normal PaCO₂ and a PaO₂ of 45 mm Hg on 80% O₂. This shows that:
o: Ventilation and oxygenation can fail separately
Oxygenation can't fail while PaCO₂ is normal
The ABG must have a sampling error
q.e: The two move independently: normal PaCO₂ with terrible PaO₂ (ARDS, shunt), or normal PaO₂ with lethal PaCO₂ (overdose).

q.q: Tidal volume on the ventilator should be based on:
q.e: VT is always set from IBW/PBW, never actual body weight.

q.q: What is the IBW formula for a MALE?
q.e: Male IBW = 50 + 2.3 × (in − 60). Female IBW = 45 + 2.3 × (in − 60) (deck); Heuer/ARDSNet use 45.5 for females.

q.q: What is the IBW of a 5'10" male?
What is the IBW of a 5'4" female (deck formula)?
A 6'0" male is being ventilated at 8 mL/kg IBW. What VT should be set?
A 5'8" female is being ventilated at 8 mL/kg IBW (deck formula). What VT should be set?
A 5'10" male with ARDS needs lung-protective ventilation at 6 mL/kg PBW. What VT is appropriate?
q.e: IBW 73 kg × 6 = 438 mL. "If you remember one number for ARDS, remember 6 mL/kg PBW."

q.q: What is the lung-protective VT for ARDS?
q.e: ARDS ≈ 6 mL/kg PBW; ARDSNet 4–6 mL/kg IBW with Pplat < 30 cm H₂O.

q.q: What VT range is used with permissive hypercapnia?
q.e: Permissive hypercapnia: 4–7 mL/kg, PaCO₂ allowed > 50 mm Hg.

q.q: A patient with ARDS has rising PIP and plateau pressure. What is the SAFEST initial adjustment?
q.e: NBRC pearl: with ↑ PIP, ↑ Pplat and ARDS, decrease VT.

q.q: What is the P50 of normal adult hemoglobin?
q.e: Hess: P50 = the PO₂ at 50% saturation; normal ≈ 27 mm Hg.

q.q: A RIGHT shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve means:
o: Hb releases O₂ more easily (higher P50)
Hb holds O₂ more tightly (lower P50)
Hb can no longer carry any O₂
The measured PaO₂ is falsely high
q.e: Right shift = ↓ affinity, ↑ P50, easier unloading.

q.q: Which set of changes shifts the curve to the RIGHT?
q.e: Hess: ↑ temp, ↑ PCO₂, ↑ 2,3-DPG or ↓ pH → right. The opposite set → left.

q.q: Which condition shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve to the LEFT?
q.e: Left shifts: alkalosis, hypothermia, ↓ PCO₂, ↓ 2,3-DPG, CO (HbCO), MetHb, and fetal hemoglobin.

q.q: What does "Left = Love" mean on the oxyhemoglobin curve?
o: Hb holds onto O₂ and won't release it
Hb releases O₂ to the tissues easily
More O₂ is delivered to the brain
q.e: Left shift = ↑ affinity, ↓ P50; tissues (especially the brain) don't receive O₂ efficiently.

q.q: Why should prolonged PaCO₂ < 30 mm Hg be avoided (unless directed by neurosurgery)?
o: It shifts the curve left, starving the brain
It shifts the curve right, causing hypoxemia
It raises ICP by dilating vessels
q.e: Left shift → cerebral tissue hypoxia → dizziness, confusion, neurologic injury.

q.q: A febrile patient's SpO₂ drops although the PaO₂ is unchanged. What explains this?
q.e: Don't mistake a right shift for a new gas-exchange problem.

q.q: Fetal hemoglobin shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve:
q.e: HbF has a left-shifted curve.

q.q: Why is the SaO₂ on a standard ABG report unreliable in CO poisoning?
o: It's calculated and can't detect COHb
q.e: Standard ABG SaO₂ is calculated from the curve. A true, measured SaO₂ requires co-oximetry (hemoximetry).

q.q: Methemoglobinemia (a complication of inhaled nitric oxide) typically produces:
o: SpO₂ ~82–86% that won't rise with O₂
Cherry-red skin and a normal SpO₂
A right-shifted curve and high P50
q.e: MetHb (Fe³⁺) can't bind O₂; the rest binds tighter (left shift). Confirm with co-oximetry; treat with methylene blue.

q.q: Dead space is BEST described as:
q.e: Dead space = wasted AIR. Shunt = wasted BLOOD.

q.q: What is the rule of thumb for ANATOMIC dead space?
o: 1 mL per pound of body weight
q.e: A 150-lb person has about 150 mL of anatomic dead space.

q.q: A patient weighs 180 lb. What is the estimated anatomic dead space?
q.e: 1 mL/lb × 180 lb = 180 mL.

q.q: What is the most common board answer for a cause of ALVEOLAR dead space?
q.e: Alveolar VD: PE (most common answer), severe hypotension, cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, excessive PEEP. Atelectasis, pneumonia and edema cause shunt.

q.q: Physiologic dead space equals:
o: Anatomic dead space + alveolar dead space
Alveolar dead space − anatomic dead space
q.e: Physiologic VD = anatomic VD + alveolar VD.

q.q: Anatomic dead space is 150 mL. What happens to VD/VT when VT falls from 500 mL to 300 mL?
q.e: VD stays constant while the breath shrinks: 150/500 = 30%; 150/300 = 50%.

q.q: What is the normal VD/VT ratio per Hess (the 202 textbook)?
q.e: Hess 0.3–0.4 (Heuer 0.25–0.35). VD/VT > 0.6–0.7 predicts weaning failure.

q.q: Which gas-exchange problem is LEAST responsive to oxygen therapy?
q.e: You can't push O₂ into a collapsed or fluid-filled alveolus. Shunt needs recruitment (PEEP, CPAP), not more FiO₂.

q.q: Which condition causes SHUNT (perfusion without ventilation)?
q.e: Shunt: atelectasis, pneumonia, ARDS, pulmonary edema. Dead space: PE, shock, excessive PEEP.

q.q: Normally, less than what percentage of blood bypasses gas exchange (physiologic shunt)?
q.e: Normal shunt < 5%.

q.q: A patient rescued from a house fire has SpO₂ 99% and PaO₂ 95 mm Hg but is confused with a headache. What should the RT do?
o: Don't trust the SpO₂ — confirm with CO-oximetry
Recheck the pulse oximeter on a different finger
q.e: CO poisoning: pulse ox reads falsely normal; PaO₂ is normal because dissolved O₂ is unaffected. Confirm with co-oximetry.

q.q: Why is PaO₂ normal in carbon monoxide poisoning?
o: PaO₂ is dissolved O₂, which CO doesn't affect
CO increases the dissolved O₂ in plasma
The PO₂ electrode cannot detect CO
q.e: CO binds hemoglobin, not plasma O₂ — hypoxia without hypoxemia.

q.q: CO poisoning causes tissue hypoxia in which two ways?
o: Less O₂ carried, and a left shift holds it
Lower PaO₂ and a right-shifted curve
New shunt and dead space in the lungs
Higher PaCO₂ and a higher pH
q.e: HbCO prevents O₂ binding and shifts the curve left, so the O₂ that is carried is held tightly.

q.q: What is the treatment for CO poisoning?
o: 100% O₂ by NRB; hyperbaric if severe
q.e: O₂ displaces CO from Hb and shortens the COHb half-life; hyperbaric O₂ greatly increases dissolved O₂.

q.q: Which equation shows why oxygenation must be judged by content, not PaO₂ alone?
q.e: Anemia and CO lower CaO₂ even with a normal PaO₂; an ABG doesn't measure carrying capacity.

sections.title: Exam Strategy & Word Play
sections.covers: Phrases that mean the same thing · special precaution words · double effect

q.q: On an exam, "bronchoprovocation test" means the same thing as:
q.e: Bronchoprovocation test = Methacholine Challenge.

q.q: A question describes a patient as a "CO₂ retainer." Which phrase means the same thing?
q.e: Chronic Hypercarbia = CO₂ Retainer.

q.q: A question asks for a device that delivers a "controlled O₂ concentration." This means:
q.e: Controlled O₂ concentration = Specific FiO₂ (e.g., an air-entrainment mask).

q.q: "Inclusion criteria" means the same thing as:
q.e: Inclusion Criteria = Indication. Exclusion Criteria = Contraindication.

q.q: "Exclusion criteria" means the same thing as:
q.e: Exclusion Criteria = Contraindication.

q.q: "Liberation parameters" refers to:
q.e: Liberation Parameters = Weaning.

q.q: On the exam, "mainstay" of therapy means:
o: Best suited for / therapy of choice
q.e: Mainstay = Best suited for / Therapy of choice.

q.q: Which terms all mean the same thing?
o: HFNC = simple nasal cannula up to 15 L
q.e: NIPPV = NPPV = NIV = BiPAP.

q.q: On the exam, SIMV means the same thing as:
q.e: SIMV = IMV on the word-play list.

q.q: PBW (predicted body weight) means the same thing as:
q.e: PBW = IBW.

q.q: "Radiolucency" on a chest x-ray refers to:
q.e: Radiolucency = Dark areas (aka Clear Lungs).

q.q: "Oxygen-induced hypoventilation" means:
q.e: Oxygen-induced Hypoventilation = Knocked out the Hypoxic Drive.

q.q: "No purposeful movement to command" means the patient is:
q.e: No purposeful movement to command = Unconscious.

q.q: A patient admitted "to the hospital for observation" goes to:
q.e: Hospital for Observation = Floor Care NOT ICU.

q.q: On the exam, HFNC refers to:
o: A regular cannula up to 15 L/min
q.e: HFNC = VapoTherm or Optiflow (Fisher & Paykel), not "HFNC up to 15 L."

q.q: "Developing COPD" is NOT the same as:
q.e: Developing COPD does NOT = Exacerbation.

q.q: A Rapid Response Team (RRT) is the same as a:
q.e: RRT = MET.

q.q: "Induction agents" on the exam means:
q.e: Induction Agents = Anesthetic Meds.

q.q: "Imbalance" (as in V/Q imbalance) means the same as:
q.e: Imbalance = Mismatch.

q.q: "Long-standing" in a question stem means:
q.e: Long-standing = Chronic.

q.q: An "expiratory balloon valve" is the same as a:
q.e: Expiratory Balloon Valve = One-way valve.

q.q: Per the study guide's word-play list, "Heart failure" is equated with cardiac arrest / cardiac failure, with which reminder?
o: It is the same as COPD
q.e: Heart Failure = Cardiac Arrest = Cardiac Failure (O₂ does NOT help!) — as written on the study guide.

q.q: On the exam, "mechanical ventilation" can refer to:
q.e: Mechanical Ventilation = Vent or BiPAP; it is NOT specific to vents only.

q.q: Which pair does the study guide warn are NOT the same?
q.e: ***Severe and Significant are NOT THE SAME!!

q.q: "Eliminate" in a question stem does NOT mean "filter." What distinction does this protect?
q.e: Eliminate does NOT mean Filter (Lungs vs. Kidneys).

q.q: "Warrants" in a question stem means:
q.e: Warrants = Justification for…

q.q: "Obliterated" on an x-ray or exam question means:
q.e: Obliterated = Blocked out / Can't see.

q.q: PISS stands for Pin Index Safety System. Its purpose is to:
o: Measure the pressure left in a cylinder
Regulate the flow rate from a cylinder
Humidify the gas leaving a cylinder
q.e: PISS prevents mistaken use of the wrong gas on small cylinders.

q.q: "Hasten" means:
q.e: Hasten = Quick to do something (see Double Effect).

q.q: A question says a treatment plan change was suggested. Why must you be careful?
o: A plan change is not the same as an order
A plan change is always an actual order
Plan changes never need an order
Only the RT can change orders
q.e: Changes to treatment plan and "actual orders" are NOT the same.

q.q: "Aggressive pain control" in a question stem means:
o: Adequate pain control, not too much
q.e: Aggressive pain control does NOT mean too much meds.

q.q: Under the principle of DOUBLE EFFECT, what makes giving a large morphine dose to a terminally ill patient permissible?
o: The intent is pain relief, not death
The intent is to hasten death
q.e: The "Intention" is the difference. Intending to relieve pain (foreseeing, not intending, hastened death) is permissible; intending death is not.

q.q: A physician gives a large morphine dose INTENDING to end a terminally ill patient's life. Under double effect, this is:
o: Impermissible, because the intent is to cause death
Permissible, because the patient is terminal
Permissible if the dose is standard
q.e: Intending to bring about death is impermissible, even with the same dose.

q.q: Which exam strategy does the study guide stress most about changing answers?
o: Choose "all of the above" when unsure
q.e: TRUST YOUR "FIRST" INSTINCT — many students wish they had stayed with their first choice. Also: NBRC WORLD ONLY.
